en: The Blessed Lord said: O son of Kuntī, this body is designated as the "field" (kṣetra).
Those who know this declare that he who understands this is the "knower of the field" (kṣetrajña). //1//
Śrīdhara:
Since it was stated that "I am the deliverer of devotees from saṃsāra," the knowledge of reality (tattva-jñāna) is now proclaimed for the sake of accomplishing that promise.
"I shall become their deliverer from the ocean of death and worldly existence before long, O Pārtha" (Gītā 12.7)— this was previously promised.

And since deliverance from worldly existence is not possible without self-knowledge, this chapter on the discrimination between *prakṛti* and *puruṣa* is commenced for the purpose of instructing in the knowledge of reality.

In that regard, the two natures—the lower (aparā) and the higher (parā)—which were mentioned in the seventh chapter, it is due to the failure to discriminate between them that this cycle of worldly existence (saṃsāra) occurs for the conscious element (cid-aṃśa) which has assumed the state of a living being (jīva). Furthermore, it is for the sake of the living being's experience that the Lord engages in creation and other activities by means of those two natures.

Desiring to define in reality those very two natures—which are designated by the terms "field" (kṣetra) and "knower of the field" (kṣetrajña) and are mutually distinct—the Blessed One said: "This... [referring to the verse beginning with *idam*.]
This body, the locus of experience, is called the "field" (kṣetra),
because it is the ground for the sprouting of saṃsāra.
Those who know this and conceive of it as "I" and "mine" are called "knowers of the field" (kṣetrajña).
Because they are the enjoyers of its fruit, like farmers; "those who know that" refers to those who possess the discriminative knowledge of the field and the Knower of the field. //1//
Madhusūdana:
If yogins, by means of a mind mastered through the practice of meditation, perceive that certain supreme light which is beyond attributes and devoid of action, let them see it.
But for us, may that very same indescribable blue splendor, which runs along the banks of the Yamunā, long serve as a marvel for our eyes.

The meanings of the terms *tat* and *tvam* have been explained in the first and middle hexads, respectively; however, the final hexad, which culminates in the meaning of the sentence (*vākyārtha*) and is primarily concerned with right knowledge (*samyag-dhī*), is now commenced.
In this regard, it was previously stated: "I shall become their deliverer from the ocean of the mortal cycle of birth and death" (Gītā 12.7).
And since deliverance from death, characterized as ignorance of the Self, is not possible without the knowledge of the Self, [the following is taught].

Therefore, that knowledge of the self through which there is cessation of death and saṃsāra, and by which the renunciants previously described— endowed with qualities such as non-hostility— are characterized by the knowledge of reality,
must now be explained.
And that [knowledge] has as its object precisely the non-difference of the individual soul (jīva) from the non-dual Supreme Self (paramātman).
Since all misfortune is caused by the delusion of difference regarding that [Brahman], there may arise the doubt:

"How can there be non-difference between the transmigrating individual souls (jīvas), which are distinct in every body, and the one non-transmigrating Supreme Self (paramātman)? To this, [the answer is given]: because both transmigratory existence and the state of being distinct are properties of the non-self (anātman) imagined through ignorance (avidyā).
It should not be said that the individual soul (jīva) possesses transmigratory existence or duality;

for that purpose, in this chapter, the distinction between the field (kṣetra) and the knower of the field (kṣetrajña) is established in order to demonstrate that the individual soul— the Puruṣa who is the knower of the field— is one and the same, changeless, and distinct from the fields consisting of the body, the senses, and the internal organ.

In this regard, the Blessed Lord, wishing to define the reality by means of the discrimination between those two natures—which were indicated by the terms "the lower" and "the higher" as the field in the form of earth and so forth, and the knower of the field in the form of the living soul—said:
"This body...
This body, O Kaunteya, is the abode of experience, accompanied by the senses and the internal organ.
It is called the "field" (kṣetra) because,
just as in the case of grain, the fruit of action is repeatedly produced within it.
Those who know this [body] yet still conceive the notions of "I" and "mine" are called the "knower of the field" (kṣetrajña), because— like a farmer— they are the enjoyers of its fruits.
"Those who know that" means those who know the discrimination between the field (*kṣetra*) and the knower of the field (*kṣetrajña*).

Here, by using the accusative construction in the word "is described" (*abhidhīyate*), it is stated that because the field is insentient, it possesses the status of an object (*karman*); whereas regarding the term "knower of the field," they say that because it is self-luminous, it lacks the status of an object, even though the word "iti" is used without the dual ending. This is said only by those who lack discrimination.

The Blessed One indicates this by employing a unique verbal expression and a single agentive case in one instance, in order to state that [the object] is beyond the range of perception for those with coarse vision. //1//
Viśvanātha:
Salutations to the devotion to the Blessed One, by whose grace— even from a mere fragment of her own portion—
one may abide even in knowledge and other virtues, thereby making them meaningful.
In this third hexad, knowledge mixed with devotion is described;
within that, pure devotion itself is also exalted by way of a particular stylistic turn.
In the thirteenth [chapter], the body, the individual self (jīvātman), the supreme self (paramātman),
the means of knowledge, the individual soul, and primordial nature (prakṛti) are specifically distinguished.
Thus, by the second group of six verses, the attainment of the Blessed One through exclusive devotion alone has been described.
Following that, three other forms of worship—beginning with the *ahaṃgraha* (identification) meditation—have been taught.
Now, for those practitioners of desireless *karma-yoga* mentioned in the first group of six, liberation arises precisely from knowledge mixed with devotion (*bhakti*).

And although knowledge has been stated in brief, he begins the third hexad in order to explain it further by means of the discrimination between the field (kṣetra) and the knower of the field (kṣetrajña), and so forth.
In response to the inquiry as to what the field is and who the knower of the field is, he says: "This.
This body, together with the senses, is the field, because it is the ground for the growth of saṃsāra.
He who knows that [body]—perceiving it during the state of bondage through the notions of "I" and "mine," and knowing it solely as being related to himself—[is the knower of the field].
In the state of liberation, one who is devoid of the conceit of "I" and "mine" knows [the Self] as being indeed free from any relation to itself;
they call that living being (jīva), existing in both states, the Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña).
Like a farmer, he alone is the Knower of the Field and the enjoyer of its fruit.
As it was said by the Blessed One:
"The greedy village-dwellers eat one fruit of this [tree], and the forest-dwellers eat another."
"He who knows the one who is manifold through sacrifices and consists of Māyā as the Haṃsa—he truly knows the Veda.
(BhP 11.12.23) The meaning of this is as follows: "Gṛdhras" are those who greedily desire; they are village-dwellers, bound souls, who eat the fruit of this tree, which is suffering.
Because even heaven and the like are, by their very nature, forms of suffering;
and the swans dwelling in the forest— liberated souls— consume the singular fruit of happiness, since even liberation, which is in every respect of the nature of bliss, is produced from this.

Thus, even this single tree of saṃsāra is multiform because it brings about various hells, heavens, and liberation; it is composed of illusion (māyāmaya) because it arises from the power of illusion (māyā-śakti).
Those who know it—those who, by means of venerable and worshipful gurus, know [this]—are the knowers of the field and the knower of the field (kṣetra-kṣetrajña). //1//
Baladeva:
Those principles beginning with the individual soul (jīva), which were implicitly mentioned in the first two hexads,
have their essential natures clearly purified here in this final hexad.
Since knowledge serves as the gateway to the devotion previously taught,
that knowledge concerning the body, the individual soul, and the Lord must be explained in the thirteenth chapter.
In the first six chapters, action performed without desire (niṣkāma-karma) was shown as being conducive to knowledge;
however, in the middle six chapters, the worship of the Supreme Self—designated as devotion (bhakti)—is taught, preceded by a description of His majesty.
And that [worship], by making one subject to Him alone, leads to His attainment.

However, for those such as the afflicted who worship Him, it is said that He destroys their suffering and so forth; through exclusive devotion (*aikāntya*), He is purely existent and the means of attaining Him.
Furthermore, when approached through yoga and knowledge, He is characterized primarily by His sovereignty and reveals His own nature, acting as the liberator.

Likewise, in this final group of six chapters, the world—caused by primordial matter (*prakṛti*), the individual soul (*puruṣa*), and their conjunction—as well as the essential nature of its Lord, and the natures of action, knowledge, and devotion, are all analyzed in detail.
For the sake of clarifying knowledge, in this third chapter, the natures of the body, the individual soul (*jīva*), and the Supreme Lord must be discerned.

Furthermore, the cause of the connection between the individual soul—which is distinct from the body and other such things—and the body, as well as the method for investigating that distinction, must be examined.
To explain this entire subject matter, the Blessed One said, "This... and so forth.

O Kaunteya, this body, together with the senses and the vital breaths, is designated as the "field" (kṣetra) by those who know the truth, because it is the ground for the growth of the enjoyments— such as pleasure and pain— to be experienced by the individual soul (jīva), the enjoyer.

Although this body is perceived by the ignorant through the distinction of the self as "I am a god," "I am a human," or "I am fat," one who understands that it is distinct from the self— like a bed or a seat— and serves as the means for the self's experience and liberation, [is a knower of the field].

Those who know the field and the Knower of the field— those who possess knowledge of their respective natures— call that [Self], which is distinct from the body as its knower, the "Knower of the field" (kṣetrajña).
The fact that the body is the means for experience and liberation has been stated in the Śrī Bhagavad-gītā:
The greedy village-dwellers eat one fruit of this [tree], while those who dwell in the forest eat another;
and the swans, through their sacrifices, enjoy that which is manifold in form.
"He who knows that which consists of illusion knows the Veda. Thus [it is said].
But the Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña) is not one who asserts the body to be the self, because of the absence of knowledge regarding that [body], which is itself the field. //1//
And know Me also as the Knower of the Field in all fields, O Bharata;
the knowledge of the Field and the Knower of the Field—that is considered by Me to be true knowledge. (13.2)
Śrīdhara: Thus, the nature of the transmigrating being has been described.

Now, he states its ultimate, non-transmigrating nature with the words "the Knower of the Field" (kṣetrajña). Know that very Knower of the Field, the transmigrating individual soul (jīva), who in reality pervades all fields, to be none other than Me.

Since my own nature has been described by the scriptural statement "That thou art" (*tattvam asi*) through the aspect of consciousness (*cid-aṃśa*) thus indicated, He praises that knowledge for the sake of showing respect:
"This very knowledge of the distinction between the field (*kṣetra*) and the knower of the field (*kṣetrajña*), because it is the cause of liberation, is considered by Me to be true knowledge;
any other is merely vain scholarship."
The meaning is: "because they are the cause of bondage. As it has been said:
"That is action which does not lead to bondage;
that is knowledge which leads to liberation."
"Any other action leads to weariness; knowledge is one thing, while skill in the arts is another," said Madhusūdana.

Having thus described the Knower of the Field (*kṣetrajña*) as self-luminous and distinct from the body, senses, and so forth, he declares his ultimate reality to be identity with the non-transmigrating Supreme Self in the words "the Knower of the Field also. That single Knower of the Field who exists in all fields, whose nature is self-luminous consciousness, and who is eternal and all-pervading— know, that is, realize, him as Me, the Lord, who am free from transmigratory existence and whose nature is the non-dual bliss of Brahman, by abandoning the form of the Knower of the Field characterized by the transmigratory attributes of agency, enjoyership, and the like, which are superimposed by ignorance.
O Bhārata!

Thus, the field (*kṣetra*) is falsely imagined through *māyā*, whereas the Knower of the Field (*kṣetrajña*) is the ultimate reality (*paramārtha-satya*), the substratum for that delusion; this is the [distinction] between the field and the Knower of the Field.

That very [knowledge] is what I consider to be "jñāna" because it is the means to liberation; it is of the nature of light that opposes ignorance (avidyā). Anything else, however, is merely "ajñāna" because it is opposed to that. This is the intended meaning. Regarding this point—that the distinction between the individual soul (jīva) and the Lord (īśvara) is due to ignorance (āvidyaka), while their non-difference is ultimate (pāramārthika)—the arguments have been described by the authors of the Bhāṣya.
However, we have not set them forth here, both for fear of excessive prolixity in this treatise and because they have already been explained by us in many ways previously. //2//
Viśvanātha:
Thus, the status of being the Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña) has been stated for the individual self (jīvātman) through its knowledge of the Field;

however, because the Supreme Self is the Knower of all Fields in their entirety even more than that, He declares its status as the Knower of the Field with the words "the Knower of the Field" (kṣetrajñam).
Know Me, the Supreme Self, as the Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña) abiding as the controller in all fields.
While that status of being the Knower of the Field does not belong in its entirety to each individual living being who is a knower of their own field,
the distinction must be understood that for Me alone, being the Knower of all fields is complete in its totality.

In response to the inquiry "What is knowledge?", he says: "The knowledge of the field-knower (kṣetrajña) together with the field (kṣetra)—that is, the knowledge of the individual self (jīvātman), the supreme self (paramātman), and [the relationship between] the field, the individual self, and the supreme self—this alone is my view and is approved by me. Regarding this, because of a contradiction with the text, the position of monism (ekātmavāda) should not be followed through any other interpretation. //2//

Baladeva: The status of being the Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña) has been stated with respect to the individual soul (jīvātman) through its knowledge of the field. Now, he states that same status with respect to the Supreme Self: "And know Me also as the Knower of the Field. O Bhārata, know Me also to be the Knower of the Field within all fields.
The word *api* is used here for emphasis.

The individual souls (*jīvas*) are "knowers of the field" (*kṣetrajñas*) because they know their respective fields—that is, the means for their own enjoyment and liberation—just as subjects [know their domains].
But I, the Lord of all, am alone the knower of all those fields, knowing that they are all to be sustained by me; thus, the meaning is that I am like a king.
Even for the Lord of All and the Lord of the Field, there is the state of being the Knower of the Field—
for the fields are indeed the bodies,
and the seed is both the auspicious and the inauspicious.
The one whose self is yoga knows those [objects]; therefore, he is called the Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña).
This is according to such Smṛti passages as these.
In response to the inquiry "What is knowledge?", he says: "The Knower of the Field.
The two knowers of the field (kṣetrajñau) together with the field are the individual soul (jīva) and the Supreme (para); these are the "field and the knower of the field" (kṣetra-kṣetrajñau).
The knowledge that arises from the mutual discernment of those two together with that [Self] is alone considered by me to be true knowledge;
otherwise, it is ignorance—this is the meaning.
Here, this should be understood: because Prakṛti, Jīva, and Īśvara possess the respective attributes of being the object of enjoyment, the enjoyer, and the controller.

The author of the Sūtras states that even though these [principles] are mutually conjoined, there is no confusion of their respective attributes, just as in the case of the colors of a variegated cloth; thus he says: "But not because of the existence of an illustration" (*na tu dṛṣṭānta-bhāvāt*).
Furthermore, the Śrutis declare that primordial matter (*prakṛti*) and the others possess their own distinct attributes.
Having realized the Self and the Impeller as distinct, he, being favored by Him, thereafter attains immortality.
There are two unborn ones: the Knower and the Unknowing, the Lord and the Unlord; the Unborn is one.
Indeed, there are two unborn ones, joined with the purpose of the enjoyer and the object of enjoyment:
the perishable Pradhāna and the immortal imperishable Hara;
the one God rules over both the perishable and the self (the individual soul). (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 1.9–10)
Having understood the enjoyer, the object of enjoyment, and the impeller— all this that has been declared as the threefold Brahman—
one understands the single, unborn [nature] which is red, white, and black.
While she creates many offspring of similar form, one unborn being lies beside her, delighting in her;
another unborn being abandons her once her enjoyment has been exhausted. [Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 4.5]
"The Lord of Pradhāna and Kṣetrajña, the Master of the Guṇas" (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 6.16), and so forth.

Here too, His distinctness from the Supreme Person (Puruṣottama) is established in relation to the pair consisting of the Field (kṣetra) and the Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña), which are understood by the terms "the Perishable" (kṣara) and "the Imperishable" (akṣara).

The Lord will say, "These two persons... and so forth; therefore, the knowledge of *prakṛti* and the rest as distinct from one another, even though they are mutually conjoined, is the ultimate reality (*tāttvika*).

As for the proponent of monism who relies on the perception of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) in the passage "Know Me also as the Knower of the Field" (*kṣetrajña*), [he argues that] this being, who is in fact the Lord of all, appears as the Knower of the Field only through ignorance (*avidyā*), just as [the nature of] a rope [is perceived falsely].
This is like the state of being a serpent [superimposed] upon a rope.

To remove that [delusion], there is this statement of Hari, the most authoritative person: "And Me, the Knower of the Field" (Gītā 13.2). Just as the delusion of being a serpent ceases from the authoritative statement, "This is a rope, not a serpent," so too the delusion of being the Knower of the Field [ceases] from this statement.
The claim that [the soul] perishes has indeed been refuted precisely because such a thing cannot be taught; this should be understood from the commentary on the verse beginning with "dehino 'smin.
However, the following explanation is more appropriate:
the word "ca" (and) serves to include the "field" (kṣetra) in the aggregate.

"Know both the field and the knower of the field to be Me alone; because their existence and activity are dependent on Me and because they are pervaded by Me, know them to have Me as their very self. Thus it has been said regarding the field and the knower of the field.

Because the activities of those two [the body and the senses] are dependent upon Me and they are of My very nature, that knowledge which perceives them as such is considered by Me to be true knowledge; anything other than this is not considered knowledge.
(BhG 13.3) That field—what it is, of what nature, what its transformations are, and from whence it arises—[is now to be described].
Listen to me as I describe briefly who he is and what his power is. //3//

Śrīdhara: Although it is intended there that *prakṛti*, divided into twenty-four categories, is the field (*kṣetra*), nevertheless, since non-discrimination (*aviveka*) is clearly manifested through the sense of "I" only when that [prakṛti] has been transformed into the form of the body, this statement—
"this body is the field," and so forth— was spoken for the purpose of discriminating that [body].
Intending to elaborate upon this, he makes a formal declaration with the word "tat" (that):
that which was called by me the "field" (kṣetra) is the field whose essential nature is insentient, having the character of the perceptible and so forth;
and as to what it is like, it possesses attributes such as desire and the rest.

That which undergoes modification—that is, that which is endowed with such modifications as those of the sense organs and so forth; and from what it arises—from the conjunction of primordial matter (prakṛti) and the spirit (puruṣa);
and "that" [which] refers to the various modes, such as the distinctions between the immobile and the mobile.
The meaning is "divided.

Now, hear from me in brief all that regarding the nature and power of that Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña)—what his essential form is, what his majesty is, and with what powers he is endowed through the possession of inconceivable sovereignty. //3//
Madhusūdana begins to explain the meaning of what was stated in brief with the words "That field" (*tat kṣetram*).

That which was previously called "this body" (*tad idaṃ śarīram*)—the field consisting of the aggregate of insentient things—is by its very nature characterized as insentient, objective, limited, and so forth; it possesses such attributes as desire and the like, and undergoes such transformations.
That which is endowed with the modifications of the senses and so forth;

and from whatever cause a particular effect arises—this is the ellipsis. Alternatively, it refers to that which comes into being from the conjunction of primordial nature (prakṛti) and the spirit (puruṣa).
The word "yat" (which) means that which is divided by various distinctions such as the immobile and the mobile;
here, because the particle "ca" is used without restriction, a collective inclusion of all [distinctions] is to be understood.
And that [nature] belongs to the two—the field and the knower of the field—which, by their very essence, have the nature of self-luminous consciousness and bliss.

And hear from my words—in brief, that is, concisely—the true nature of the field and the knower of the field, characterized by all these specific attributes: its power, the powers produced by limiting conditions (upādhi), and the potencies belonging to it.
The meaning is: having heard it, you should comprehend it. //13.3//
Viśvanātha begins to explain the meaning that was stated in brief: "That field" is the body, which consists of an aggregate of the great elements, the vital breaths, the sense organs, and so forth;
"of such a kind" means possessing attributes such as various desires and the like.
That which is subject to modification (*vikāri*) means that which is endowed with modifications such as those of enemies, loved ones, and so forth;
and that which has arisen from the conjunction of *prakṛti* and *puruṣa*;
and "that which" (*yat*) means that which is divided by various distinctions such as the immobile and the mobile—this is the meaning.
That *kṣetrajña* is the individual self (*jīvātman*) and the supreme self (*paramātman*).
The neuter form "yat tat" is a single-remainder compound (*eka-śeṣa*), according to the rule that "a neuter [word] [is used with] non-neuters [in the same case], even if not in the singular.
"In brief" means by way of summary. //3//

Baladeva says: In order to clarify the meaning briefly stated, he says "That" (tat). That field is the body; and as to what substance it is, of what nature it is, what its substratum is, what its modifications are—i.e., endowed with which modifications—and from what cause it has arisen, and for what purpose it exists.
The word "yat" (that which) refers to the essential nature (*svarūpa*).

And that Knower of the Field (*kṣetrajña*)—characterized as the individual soul (*jīva*) and characterized as the Supreme Lord (*pareśa*)—is whatever its essential nature may be, whatever its power (*prabhāva*), and whatever its capacity (*śakti*) may be.
[The neuter gender is used] according to the rule: "A neuter [word] remains neuter when combined with a non-neuter [word], and it takes the singular number when the referents are different. //3//
It has been sung by the seers in many ways, in various distinct Vedic hymns, and also in the words of the Brahma-sūtras, which are reasoned and definitive. (13.4)
Śrīdhara: In response to the inquiry, "By whom was this taught in detail, such that this is a summary?", he says, "by the sages" (*ṛṣibhiḥ*).

By the sages, such as Vasiṣṭha and others, [it] has been sung—that is, described—in many ways in the Yoga-śāstras as the subject matter of meditation (*dhyāna*), concentration (*dhāraṇā*), and so forth, in forms such as Virāja and others.

It has been sung in many ways through various and diverse Vedic hymns (*chandobhiḥ*) concerning obligatory, occasional, and optional rites, etc., in the form of numerous deities to be worshipped and so forth.
By the "threads" (sūtra) and "words" (pada) of Brahman. They are called *brahma-sūtrāṇi* because Brahman is threaded or indicated by them.

These refer to the Upaniṣadic statements such as, "From which indeed these beings are born" (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 3.1.1), which are intent upon defining Brahman through its extrinsic characteristics (*taṭastha-lakṣaṇa*).

And likewise, Brahman is "approached" (pad), meaning it is reached or directly known through these; thus, the words such as "Brahman is Truth, Knowledge, Infinite" refer to its essential nature (*svarūpa-lakṣaṇa*).
And by these, it has been sung in many ways.
Furthermore, there are reasoned arguments: "In the beginning, my dear, this was Being alone; how could Being be born from Non-being? [Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.2.1].

Likewise, [the text says]: "For who indeed could inhale, who could exhale, if this bliss were not in the ether? For he alone causes bliss" (TaittU 2.7.1), and so forth—[these are] supported by reasoning.
Who else could perform the activity of inhalation (*apāna*)?
The meaning of the two scriptural phrases is: "Who could breathe, or who could perform the functions of the vital breath?
[The word] "viniścitaiḥ" means by those [scriptural passages] which establish an unambiguous meaning through the unity of purpose between their opening and concluding sections.
Thus, that which has been explained at length by these [passages] is difficult to summarize; I shall, however, tell it to you in brief.
The meaning is: "Listen to that.
Alternatively, the *Brahma-sūtras* beginning with "Then, therefore, the desire to know Brahman" (1.1.1) are taken here;
these very [sūtras] are called "words" (*padāni*) because Brahman is reached (*padyate*) or ascertained by means of them.

The meaning is that these reasons are established by means of arguments such as "Because of seeing, [the Self is not that which is] not based on scripture" (VS 1.1.5) and "The one consisting of bliss [is Brahman] because of repetition" (VS 1.1.13).
The rest is the same. //4//
Madhusūdana:

In response to the inquiry, "By whom was this taught in detail such that this is now a summary?", he speaks in praise for the purpose of inspiring the intellects of the listeners, saying "by the sages" (*ṛṣibhiḥ*).
It has been sung—that is, described in many ways—as the object of *dhāraṇā* and *dhyāna* in the Yoga scriptures by the sages, such as Vasiṣṭha and others.
By this, its being the subject matter of the Yoga-śāstra is stated.

It has been sung separately and with discrimination by various Vedic hymns (*chandas*)—namely the *Ṛg* and other mantras—and by the Brāhmaṇas, concerning the subjects of obligatory, occasional, and optional rites;
by this, its being the subject matter of the Karma-kāṇḍa is stated.

And by the words *brahma-sūtra*: Brahman is "sūtried" (strung together) or indicated; these are called *brahma-sūtras* because by means of them Brahman is set forth with some degree of mediation—as in: "From which indeed these beings are born;
by which, once born, they live;
into which they enter at their departure."
Thus, by means of those Brahma-sūtras and words— such as [TaittU 3.1.1], which refer to extrinsic characteristics (*taṭastha-lakṣaṇa*),

and such as "Brahman is truth, knowledge, and infinite" (*satyaṃ jñānam anantaṃ brahma*), which refer to intrinsic characteristics (*svarūpa-lakṣaṇa*) because Brahman is directly understood (*sākṣāt pratipadyate*) through them.

"By those who provide reasons"—having introduced the materialist view by first stating, "In the beginning, my dear, this was Being alone, one only, without a second" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.2.1), and then presenting the nihilistic position, "Now some say that in the beginning this was Non-being alone, one only, without a second; from that Non-being, Being was born," [the Teacher] said, "But how indeed, my dear, could it be so? How could Being come from Non-being?"

It has also been sung in many ways by those who are certain, establishing such arguments as "it is born" and so forth, and demonstrating a meaning free from doubt through the unity of purpose between the introduction and the conclusion.
By this, its status as the subject matter of the *jñāna-kāṇḍa* (the section on knowledge) is stated.
The meaning is: "Having thus explained the true nature of the field and the knower of the field at great length, I shall now tell it to you in brief; listen to that.
Alternatively, it is a *karmadhāraya* compound meaning "the aphorisms of Brahman" (*brahma-sūtra*) which are also "words" (*pada*);

therein, the "aphorisms of knowledge" (*vidyā-sūtra*) are such as "One should meditate [on the Self] as 'I am the Self'" (*ātmety evopāsīta*), and the "aphorisms of ignorance" (*avidyā-sūtra*) are such as "He does not know, like a beast" (*na sa veda yathā paśuḥ*). It is sung by these. //4//
Viśvanātha:

In response to the inquiry, "By whom was this taught in detail, of which this is a summary?", he says: "By the sages," such as Vasiṣṭha and others, "in the Yoga-śāstras"; "by the meters," that is, by the Vedas.

The Brahma-sūtras are those beginning with "Now, therefore, the inquiry into Brahman" (atha-ato brahma-jijñāsā, 1.1.1); they are called *sūtras* because Brahman is strung together (*padyate*) or known by means of them. Furthermore, by what kind of means? By those that are "possessed of reasons" (*hetumat*).

[The Lord says: "Because of seeing" (Brahma Sūtra 1.1.5), "The one consisting of bliss [is Brahman] because of repetition" (Brahma Sūtra 1.1.13)—by means of these logically sound and specifically determined conclusions.
Baladeva: In response to the expectation—"By whom has this true nature of the field and the knower of the field been explained in detail, which you now state in brief?"—he says, "By the sages."
This nature of the field and so forth has been sung in many ways by the sages, such as Parāśara and others:
"O King, I, you, and likewise others, are carried away by the elements; even this entire aggregate of beings, having fallen into the flow of the *guṇas*, is passing along."
O Lord of the Earth, these qualities such as *sattva* and the rest are indeed subject to *karma*;
and that *karma*, accumulated through ignorance, exists in all living beings without exception.
"The Self is pure, imperishable, tranquil, devoid of qualities, and beyond primordial nature;
it neither increases nor decreases, being one and the same among all living beings"—
thus by such passages as these.
Likewise, that has been sung in many ways through all the various Vedic meters; specifically, in the Yajur-veda branch,

from the passage beginning with "From this very Self, space was produced" (TaittU 2.1.3) up to the end with "Brahman is the tail, the support" (TaittU 2.5.1), there are the five sheaths consisting of food, vital breath, mind, consciousness, and bliss.
Among those persons mentioned, the triad beginning with the one consisting of food (*annamaya*) is insentient and constitutes the nature of the field (*kṣetra*).

Distinct from that is the individual soul (*jīva*), consisting of consciousness (*vijñānamaya*), who is its enjoyer; this is the nature of the individual knower of the field (*jīva-kṣetrajña*). And distinct from that is the one consisting of bliss (*ānandamaya*), the innermost of all; thus the nature of the Lord as the knower of the field (*īśvara-kṣetrajña*) has been described.
In this same manner, one should seek [the truth] within the other Vedas. The true nature of that [Brahman] is sung through words and sentences in the form of the Brahma-sūtras;
among these, the nature of the field (kṣetra) is established by such passages as "In them, space is not [produced], because it is not heard [to be so]" (Vs. 2.3.1).
The nature of the individual soul (jīva) is established by the sūtra "The self is not [the body], because of scripture" (Vs. 2.3.18) and so forth;
the nature of the Lord (īśvara) is established by the sūtra "But that [is the self] because of scripture regarding the Supreme" (Vs. 2.3.39) and so forth.
The rest is clear.
The great elements, ego-consciousness, intellect, and the unmanifest; the ten senses and the one [mind], and the five objects of the senses. (13.5)
Desire, aversion, pleasure, pain, the composite whole, volition, and fortitude—this is declared to be the field in brief, along with its modifications. //6//
Śrīdhara: Regarding that, he describes the nature of the field (kṣetra) in two verses beginning with "the great elements" (mahābhūtāni).
The great elements are the five, beginning with earth;
ego (ahaṅkāra) is that which serves as their cause.
Intellect (*buddhi*) is the Great Principle (*mahat-tattva*), whose nature is discernment (*vijñāna*).
The Unmanifest (*avyakta*) is the Root Nature (*mūla-prakṛti*).
The external sense organs (*indriya*) are the ten, consisting of the organs of cognition and the organs of action.
And there is the one mind.

Furthermore, the five objects of the senses—sound and the rest—are of the nature of the subtle elements (*tanmātra*) alone; having become manifest as the specific qualities of space and the other [elements], they constitute the five sense-objects. Thus, the twenty-four principles (*tattva*) have been explained. //5//
"Iccha" refers to desire and so forth, which are well known. "Saṅghāta" is the body. "Cetanā" is a mental activity consisting of cognition.
Fortitude is steadfastness.
If these qualities, beginning with joy (hā), are not attributes of the self because they are perceptible,
then they must be attributes of the mind alone.
Therefore, they are indeed included within the field (*kṣetra*).
This is also an illustration for *saṅkalpa* (volition) and the rest.

Thus says the Śruti: "Desire, volition, doubt, faith, lack of faith, steadfastness, lack of steadfastness, shame, intelligence, and fear—all these are nothing but the mind" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.5.3).
By this, the characteristics of the field as they were asserted by the phrase "of such a kind" have been shown.

"This field, together with its modifications—that is, accompanied by the modifications of the senses and so forth—has been briefly described to you by me"; thus concludes the description of the field. //6//
Madhusūdana:
Having thus inspired Arjuna’s interest, he first describes the nature of the field (kṣetra) in two verses.
The "great elements" are the five, beginning with earth.
Ego (ahaṅkāra) is its cause, characterized by self-conceit (abhimāna).
Intellect (buddhi) is the cause of ego, the principle of the Great One (mahat-tattva), characterized by determination (adhyavasāya).
The Unmanifest (avyakta) is its cause; consisting of the qualities of sattva, rajas, and tamas, it is the Primal Matter (pradhāna), the cause of all things, which is not the effect of anything.
The particle *eva* serves to restrict the sense to the nature [of the matter].
The nature is eightfold in this very extent.
The word *ca* has the sense of a conjunction of distinct categories.
Thus, it has been explained according to the Sāṅkhya doctrine.
For the followers of the Upaniṣads, however, the unmanifest (avyakta) is the undifferentiated, indefinable power of the Supreme Lord called Māyā;
as it is said: "My Māyā is difficult to overcome."
At the beginning of creation, there is the intellect (*buddhi*), which is the act of seeing that [Primal Matter] as its object;
following that seeing, there is the ego-sense (*ahaṅkāra*), which is the volition "May I become many";
from that, the production of the five elements occurs in the sequence beginning with space. This is not [the case].

It is established that the unmanifest (avyakta), the great (mahat), and the ego (ahaṅkāra)—which are established in the Sāṅkhya—are not accepted by the followers of the Upaniṣads on the grounds of their lack of scriptural authority (*aśabdatva*) and other reasons.

Rather, it is the Unmanifest as taught in the Śruti that they accept, according to the passages: "One should know Māyā as Prakṛti and the Great Lord as the wielder of Māyā" (ŚvetU 4.10) and "Those who have attained the yoga of meditation beheld the power of the Divine Self, hidden by its own qualities" (ŚvetU 1.3). This is the Unmanifest.
"That it thought" refers to the intellect (*buddhi*) whose nature is reflection.
"May I be many; may I procreate" refers to the ego (*ahaṅkāra*) whose nature is the volition to become manifold.
"From that very Self, indeed, space was produced."
From space comes air;
from air, fire; from fire, water.
"From water, earth"—thus the five elements are established by Vedic revelation (*śruti*). This position alone is the most excellent.

As for the eleven organs: there are the five sense organs known as hearing, touch, sight, taste, and smell; and the five organs of action known as speech, hands, feet, anus, and genitals. These are they.
And there is one mind, consisting of volition and conceptualization;

and there are five objects of the senses—sound, touch, form, taste, and smell—which are the objects of the sense organs insofar as they are to be known, and of the organs of action insofar as they are to be performed.
These the Sāṅkhyas declare to be the twenty-four principles (tattvas). //5//

Desire (*kāma*) and passion (*rāga*) are said to be a mental modification (*citta-vṛtti*) consisting of longing—of the nature of "may this be mine"—directed toward pleasure or its means. Hatred (*dveṣa*), anger (*krodha*), and envy (*īrṣyā*) are said to be a mental modification opposed to such longing—of the nature of "may this not be mine"—directed toward pain or its means.
Pleasure (*sukha*) is a mental modification that has become the object of unconditional desire, which has dharma as its specific cause, and which manifests the bliss of the Supreme Self.
Pain is a mental modification that has become the object of non-specific hatred; it has unrighteousness (*adharma*) as its specific cause.
The aggregate (*saṃghāta*) is the body together with the sense organs, which is a transformation of the five gross elements.
Consciousness (*cetanā*) is a mental modification known as cognition (*jñāna*), which manifests the knowledge of one's own nature and has the means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*) as its common cause.
Fortitude (*dhṛti*) is the effort that serves as the cause for supporting the body and senses when they have become dejected.
This is an illustration; it includes the apprehension of desire and all other attributes of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*).
Thus says the Śruti: "Desire, resolve, doubt, faith, fortitude, modesty, intelligence..."

The statement, "Fear—all this is indeed mind" (BAU 1.5.3), declares that desire and the other effects are attributes of the mind by way of non-difference from their material cause (*upādāna*), just as a clay pot is non-different from its cause, clay.

This entire manifest world, from the great elements down to fortitude, is insentient; because it is illuminated by the Knower of the Field (*kṣetrajña*) acting as witness, it is not of the nature of that Self. Thus, the "Field" (*kṣetra*)—the insentient object of illumination—is summarized and described.
Indeed, the Lokāyatikas maintain that the conscious knower of the field (kṣetrajña) is merely the aggregate of the body and the senses;
the Sugatas hold that consciousness—momentary cognition alone—is the self;
and the Naiyāyikas state that desire, aversion, effort, pleasure, pain, and cognition are the marks (liṅga) of the self.

How then is it that all this is the field alone? To this he says: "with its modifications" (*sa-vikāram*). "Modification" (*vikāra*) is defined by etymologists as transformation (*pariṇāma*), beginning with birth and ending with destruction.

This [universe], beginning with the great elements (*mahābhūta*) and ending with the sustaining power (*dhṛti*), is accompanied by that [consciousness] and is subject to modification; therefore, it is not the witness of modifications. This is because it is impossible for it to perceive its own birth and destruction by itself.

Furthermore, since it is logically untenable for other things to perceive their own attributes without perceiving themselves, and because there is a contradiction between the agent and the object if one were to perceive oneself by oneself, the witness of all modifications must indeed be unchanging.
Thus it has been said:
"Without undergoing modification, one cannot be a sufferer; how can there be witnesshood for that which is subject to change?
Since I am the witness of thousands of modifications of the intellect, I am changeless.
Thus, the meaning is that being subject to modification alone is the characteristic of the field (*kṣetra*), and not the specific enumeration [of its attributes]. //6//
Viśvanātha: Regarding that, he states the essential nature of the field (*kṣetra*): the great elements, beginning with space; the ego (*ahaṅkāra*), which is their cause;
and the intellect (*buddhi*), which is the principle of the Great (*mahat-tattva*) consisting of discernment.

The unmanifest (avyakta), which is primordial nature (prakṛti), is the cause of the ego-sense (ahaṅkāra); it is also the cause of the principle of the Great One (mahat-tattva). The sense organs are the ten beginning with hearing, along with the single mind (manas).
The five objects of the senses are the domains of the senses, such as sound and so forth; thus, [the aggregate] consists of these twenty-four principles (*tattva*).
Desire and the rest are well known.
The "composite" (*saṅghāta*) is the body, which is a transformation of the five gross elements.

Volition (*cetanā*) is a mental modification consisting of the nature of cognition; steadfastness (*dhṛti*), fortitude (*dhairya*), desire (*icchā*), and so forth are likewise exclusively attributes of the mind and not attributes of the Self.
Therefore, they fall entirely within the domain of the field (*kṣetra*).
This [mention of volition] is also an illustration for resolve (*saṅkalpa*) and the rest.
And so says the Śruti: "Desire, resolve, doubt, faith, steadfastness, shame, intelligence, and fear—all this is indeed the mind" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.5.3).
By this, the attributes of the field (*kṣetra*) as proposed by the phrase "of whatever kind" have been shown.
This is the field together with its modifications.
Accompanied by the six transformations beginning with birth. //5-6//

Baladeva: With the half-verse beginning "That field which... and so forth, he states the nature of the field as promised; then, with the two verses beginning "The great elements...", he explains it. The five great elements (mahābhūtāni) are space and the rest; ego (ahaṅkāra) is their cause, being the *tāmasa* state known as *bhūtādi*; intellect (*buddhi*) is its cause, being the "Great One" (*mahat*) characterized primarily by knowledge; the unmanifest (*avyakta*) is its cause, being *pradhāna* in the state of the three qualities (*triguṇa*). The senses consist of the five beginning with hearing and the five beginning with speech; these are situated between *bhūtādi* and space and the other elements.

The meaning is as follows: the subtle elements (*tanmātra*) of sound and so forth, having become manifest as the specific qualities of ether and the other elements, are the gross objects of perception grasped by the five senses, such as the ear.
In this way, the "field" (*kṣetra*) should be understood as consisting of twenty-four principles (*tattva*).
The four beginning with desire (*icchā*) are well known; this is an illustration for those beginning with volition (*saṅkalpa*).

These mental states—desire, volition, doubt, faith, steadfastness, modesty, intelligence, and fear—are [qualities of the mind], according to the Śruti: "Desire, volition, doubt, faith, steadfastness, modesty, intelligence, and fear.
Even though desire and the rest are qualities of the Self, as heard in such passages as "He who is the Self" and "He whose desires are true, whose volitions are true," [they are nevertheless mental].

From the statement in the *Sahasranāmastotra*, "The person who desires [to recite]," and from what will be said later, that "the person is called the cause for the experience of pleasure and pain," nevertheless,
because it is manifested through the door of the mind, it possesses the nature of a mental attribute (*manodharma*).
Therefore, it is included within the field (*kṣetra*).
The "composite" (*saṅghāta*) is the body as a transformation of the elements (*bhūta-pariṇāma*).
And its meaning is that it has arisen as the substratum for the conscious individual soul (*jīva*), who possesses consciousness and strives for both enjoyment and liberation.

In this context, "substances such as *pradhāna*" refers to the initiators of the field; "and what" refers to the sense organs such as hearing which are dependent upon the ear; "of what kind" refers to desire and so forth, which are the effects of the field;
and "whose modifications" refers to consciousness and fortitude.
Regarding the phrase "yataś ca" (and from which), the word "saṅghātaḥ" (the aggregate) follows. The word "yat" (that which) has been explained above.
This field, together with its modifications—that is, endowed with the six transformations beginning with birth—has been illustrated and described. //5–6//
Absence of pride, absence of hypocrisy, non-violence, forbearance, straightforwardness, service to the teacher, purity, steadfastness, and self-restraint. (13.7)
Detachment from the objects of the senses, as well as freedom from egoism, and the constant contemplation of the evils of birth, death, old age, disease, and suffering. //8//
Non-attachment and absence of possessiveness toward children, wife, home, and so forth; and constant equanimity of mind amidst the occurrence of the pleasant and the unpleasant. //9//
And unwavering devotion to Me through the yoga of exclusive dedication;
resorting to solitary places; and a distaste for the assembly of worldly people. (10)
Constancy in the knowledge of the Self and the vision of the purpose of the knowledge of reality—this is declared to be knowledge;
that which is otherwise than this is ignorance. //11//

Śrīdhara: Now, intending to describe in detail the pure Knower of the Field (*kṣetrajña*), who is to be known as distinct from the Field (*kṣetra*) whose characteristics have been stated, [the Lord] declares the means for attaining pure knowledge with five verses beginning with "Humility" (*amānitvam*). Humility is the absence of praising one's own virtues.
Sincerity is the absence of hypocrisy;
non-violence is the avoidance of harming others;
and patience is the quality of endurance.
Straightforwardness is the absence of crookedness;
service to the teacher is attendance upon a true guru;
and purity is both external and internal.
In that regard, external purification is by means of earth, water, and so forth, while internal purification is the washing away of the impurities of passion and the like.
And thus says the Śruti:
Purity is said to be twofold: external and internal;
the external is traditionally held to consist of earth and water.
"Purity of being as well as inner [purity].
Thus, steadfastness is the single-minded devotion of one who has entered the path of the virtuous;
self-restraint is the control of the body.
"This is declared to be knowledge"—this is the syntactical connection with the fifth [verse].
And what is meant by "in me"?
It means in Me, the Supreme Lord,
through non-dual yoga— that is, by perceiving all things as the Self.
Devotion is unswerving and single-minded. A secluded place is one that produces clarity in the pure mind.
The state of one whose character is to frequent such a place is its true nature.
In the assembly or gathering of common people, there is *aratī*, which is the absence of delight.
Furthermore, regarding *adhyātma*:
knowledge that exists with reference to the self (*ātman*) is *adhyātma-jñāna*.

In that [context], "permanence" (*nityatva*) means the state of being eternal. "Reality" (*tattva*) means the state of being established as the object of the cognition of the categories of existence; such is the meaning.

The "purpose" (*artha*) of the knowledge of reality is liberation (*mokṣa*); the "vision" (*darśana*) of that [purpose] means the contemplation of liberation as being the most excellent of all things; such is the meaning.

This which has been stated as numbering twenty, beginning with "absence of pride" (amānitva) and "absence of hypocrisy" (adambhitva), is declared by Vasiṣṭha and others to be "knowledge" (jñāna), because it is a means to knowledge. That which is otherwise than this—contrary to it, such as pride and so forth—is declared to be "ignorance" (ajñāna), because it is opposed to knowledge; therefore, the meaning is that it must be abandoned in every way. //7–11//
Madhusūdana:

Having thus explained the field (kṣetra), [the Lord] now speaks of the means— beginning with "humility" (amānitva)— in the five verses preceding "That which is to be known" (jñeyaṃ yat tat), in order to explain the Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña), the witness of that field, in detail through its distinction from the field, and for the sake of making one fit for the knowledge thereof.
Self-praise is the extolling of one's own qualities, whether they actually exist or do not;
hypocrisy is the manifestation of one's own religious duties for the sake of gain, honor, and fame;
and violence is the infliction of suffering upon living beings through body, speech, and mind.

The avoidance of these has been described as humility (*amānitva*), lack of hypocrisy (*adambhitva*), and non-violence (*ahiṃsā*). *Kṣānti* (forbearance) is the endurance of another's offense by means of an unchanging mind, even when the cause for a mental disturbance—the commission of an offense by another—is encountered. *Ārjava* (straightforwardness) is the absence of crookedness; it is conduct that accords with one's heart, meaning, in short, the absence of deceiving others.
In this context, the "teacher" (ācārya) is intended as the instructor of the means to liberation, and not the one who initiates and teaches as defined by Manu.
Service to such a teacher consists in attending upon him through the practice of obedience, prostration, and so forth.

Purity (*śauca*) consists of the external cleansing of bodily impurities with earth and water, and the internal removal of mental impurities such as passion (*rāga*) and the like, by means of cultivating the antidote that perceives the defects inherent in sense objects.
Steadfastness (*sthairya*) is the repeated increase in one's application toward the means of liberation (*mokṣa-sādhana*), without abandoning it even when encountering various kinds of obstacles.

Self-restraint (*ātma-vinigraha*) is the suppression of the natural inclination of the self—the aggregate of body and senses—toward what is contrary to liberation, and its stabilization within the means of liberation itself. (7)

Furthermore: *vairāgya* (dispassion) is a mental state consisting of a lack of longing, which is opposed to attachment toward objects of the senses—whether they be perceived things such as sound and so forth, or those heard of in scripture—as enjoyments.
*Anahaṅkāra* (non-egotism) is the absence of that pride (*ahaṅkāra*), which is the conceit "I am the most excellent" arising in the mind even in the absence of self-praise.
The word *eva* (only/just) is used for the purpose of excluding [any] non-yoga.
The particle *ca* has the sense of conjunction (*samuccaya*).

Therefore, the meaning is that knowledge is declared to be the combined practice (*samucita-yoga*) of these twenty qualities beginning with humility (*amānitva*), and not the absence of even a single one of them. [This applies to] birth, which consists of emerging from the womb through the gateway of the birth canal, and death, which consists of the severing of all vital organs (*marman*).
Of old age, which consists of the cessation of wisdom, power, and vigor, as well as humiliation by others; of diseases, such as fever, dysentery, and the like;
of sufferings arising from separation from the beloved and union with the unloved, caused by internal, external, and celestial factors;
and of the bodily humors (doṣa), due to being filled with wind, bile, phlegm, excrement, urine, and so forth.

Furthermore, the contemplation (*anudarśana*) of the body’s loathsomeness is the repeated observation of its defects within the range of suffering beginning with birth and ending with old age; or alternatively, it is the contemplation of the defect consisting of the nature of suffering within the range of suffering beginning with birth and ending with disease.
And this serves as an aid to the vision of the self (*ātma-darśana*) by acting as a cause for detachment from sense objects. //8//
Furthermore: attachment (*sakti*) is mere affection based on the thought "this is mine.

Clinging (*abhiṣvaṅga*), however, is an excess of affection arising from the cultivation of non-difference, thinking "I am this very person," such that when another is happy or suffering, one thinks "I myself am happy or suffering.
The absence of these is called non-attachment (*asakti*) and non-clinging (*anabhiṣvaṅga*).

Wherein should attachment and clinging be abandoned? To this he says: "In sons, wives, houses, and so forth"—the inclusion of "and so forth" (ādi) means in all objects of affection, such as servants and others.
And one should maintain a constant and ever-present equanimity of mind, free from joy and dejection, amidst the occurrence of both the desirable and the undesirable.
"Upapatti" means attainment.
The meaning is: the absence of joy in the face of desirable attainments and the absence of despondency in the face of undesirable attainments.
The particle "ca" (and) is used for conjunction. //9//
Furthermore, devotion (*bhakti*) toward me, the Blessed Lord Vāsudeva, the Supreme Controller, is a love preceded by the knowledge of His absolute pre-eminence.

Through "exclusive yoga" (*ananya-yoga*)— the firm conviction that there is nothing superior to the Blessed Lord Vāsudeva and that He alone is our refuge— such devotion is unswerving and cannot be thwarted by any adverse cause.
That joy which is the cause of knowledge is also [the means], as it is said: "O Vāsudeva, as long as [attachment] toward me is not released through the abandonment of the body" (BhP 5.5.6).

A secluded place is one that is pure by nature or by refinement, free from impurities such as snakes and tigers, and which provides serenity by being situated on the banks of the celestial river (the Gaṅgā) and so forth; the habit of resorting to such a place is "resorting to a secluded place."
And so says the Śruti: "On a level, clean spot, free from pebbles, fire, and sand, and devoid of noise, water, and such."
"One should employ [the mind] in a place agreeable to the mind, not one that distresses the eyes, taking refuge in a cave or a windless spot" (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 2.10).
Thus [it is said regarding] the assembly or gathering of people who are averse to self-knowledge and who teach the greed for the enjoyment of sense-objects.

Dislike and lack of delight in the assembly of the virtuous—which is contrary to the knowledge of reality—is indeed improper; however, delight in that which is conducive to the knowledge of reality is entirely appropriate.
Thus it has been said:
"Association must be abandoned with one's whole being, yet it is said that this cannot be done."
One should associate with the virtuous, for association with the virtuous is indeed medicine. //10//

Furthermore: *adhyātma-jñāna* is knowledge concerning the inner self; it is the knowledge that discriminates between the Self and the non-Self. "Permanence" (*nityatva*) refers to being firmly established (*niṣṭhāvat*) in that very [discrimination].
For one who is established in discrimination becomes capable of knowing the meaning of the [great] Vedic sentences.

The "object" (*artha*) of the knowledge of reality—the direct realization (*sākṣātkāra*) "I am Brahman"—which has the Vedāntic sentences as its instrument and is the fruit of the full maturation of all the means such as impermanence and so forth, is as follows: [the following passage describes this object].

The purpose is liberation (*mokṣa*), which consists of the cessation of all suffering characterized by ignorance and its effects, and the attainment of the nature of supreme bliss; the "vision" (*darśana*) of that [purpose] is the contemplation thereof.
For when one contemplates the fruit of the knowledge of reality (*tattva-jñāna*), there will be engagement in the means to achieve it.

This group of twenty items, beginning with humility (*amānitva*) and ending with the vision of the reality of the goal of knowledge (*tattvajñānārthadarśana*), is called "knowledge" because it has knowledge as its purpose. Conversely, that which is the opposite of this—beginning with pride (*mānitva*) and so forth—is called "ignorance" because it is antagonistic to knowledge.
Therefore, the sense is that by abandoning ignorance, knowledge alone should be adopted. //11//
Viśvanātha:

Having stated the characteristics of the field (*kṣetra*), and intending to describe in detail the two knowers of the field— the individual self (*jīvātman*) and the supreme self (*paramātman*)— who are to be known as distinct from that field, [the Lord] speaks of the twenty means for that knowledge, beginning with humility (*amānitva*),
in five verses.

In this regard, eighteen qualities are common to both devotees and those possessed of knowledge; however, among these, devotees alone—through unswerving devotion by means of exclusive yoga directed toward Me—diligently cultivate that one [quality] as the specific means for the realization of the Blessed Lord.
The traditional teachers maintain that the other seventeen arise spontaneously for those who possess the aforementioned practice, and no effort is required for them.
But the last two belong exclusively to the wise.
Here, the qualities such as humility (*amānitva*) and the rest have their meanings clearly evident.
Purity (*śauca*) is both external and internal; likewise, the Smṛti states:
Purity is said to be twofold: external and internal;
the external is traditionally held to consist of earth and water.
"Purity of being as well as inner [tranquility].
Here, "self-restraint" refers to the control of the body.
"Observing the defects"—that is, repeatedly reflecting upon the fact that birth and so forth are of the nature of suffering.

Non-attachment is the relinquishing of affection for sons and others, and non-clinging is the absence of the superimposition that "I alone am happy or miserable" regarding the happiness or suffering of sons and others. It is the state of constant equanimity of mind at all times toward the occurrences and attainments of both desired and undesired worldly things. Furthermore, it is devotion unto Me—whose form is dark and beautiful—with undivided yoga, meaning unmixed with the yoga of knowledge, action, or austerity, as well as through the predominance of mixing knowledge and other such means (indicated by the word "ca").
Some say that the first [type of devotion] is to be practiced by devotees (*bhakta*) and the second by those possessing knowledge (*jñānin*);

others, however, the devotees explain, maintain that it is mentioned here in this hexad for the purpose of making known that just as exclusive devotion (*ananya-bhakti*) is the means for [attaining] love, so too is it the means for the experience of the Supreme Self.
As for the knowers of truth (*jñānin*), they hold that it is through non-dual yoga alone, by seeing the Self in all.
It must be performed every single day without fail;
it cannot be obstructed by anyone—so says Madhusūdana Sarasvatī.
Knowledge concerning the self as it exists is *adhyātma-jñāna*.
Its "perpetuity" means that it must be practiced constantly and is grounded in the purification of the categories of existence (*padārtha*).
The "purpose" of the knowledge of reality is liberation; its "vision" means contemplating it as one's own desired goal.
This twentyfold knowledge is, in general, the means for attaining the knowledge of both the individual self (*jīvātman*) and the supreme self (*paramātman*).
The uncommon knowledge of the Supreme Self shall be explained later; other than that, there is its opposite, such as pride and so forth. //7-11//

Baladeva: Now, intending to describe in detail the two types of the Knower of the Field (*kṣetrajña*) as distinct from the field (*kṣetra*) already mentioned, he states in five verses the twenty means for that knowledge, beginning with humility (*amānitva*).
Humility is the lack of expectation for one's own honor. Freedom from hypocrisy (*adambhitva*) is the absence of practicing dharma for the sake of gaining a reputation for being righteous.
Non-violence is the non-infliction of suffering upon others;
patience is the endurance of insults;
and straightforwardness is sincerity even toward those who are deceitful.
Service to the teacher is the sincere attendance upon the guru who bestows knowledge. Purity is external and internal sanctity;
and purity is said to be of two kinds.
"External as well as internal;
external is known to be by means of earth and water, while internal is the purification of one's being"— so says the Smṛti.
Steadfastness is the state of being solely devoted to the path of the virtuous.
Self-restraint is the withdrawal of the mind from sense objects that are contrary to self-inquiry.
Detachment is the absence of relish for the objects of the senses, such as sound and the rest, when they appear as adversaries.
Non-egoism (*anahaṅkāra*) is the abandonment of the conceit of self (*ātma-abhimāna*) with respect to the body and so forth.
The contemplation of defects (*doṣa*), which consist of suffering, in birth and other states is the repeated reflection upon them.
Non-attachment (*asakti*) is the relinquishing of thirst (*tṛṣṇā*) toward sons and others who are contrary to the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*).
Non-attachment toward those beings who are happy or suffering means not being fixated on their happiness or suffering.

It is the state of equanimity of mind regarding the occurrence and attainment of desired or undesired objects—those things that are favorable or unfavorable—and the absence of both elation and dejection.
This is to be maintained constantly, at all times.
Unswerving and firm devotion to Me, the Supreme Lord, consisting of hearing [the scriptures] and so forth; service to My devotees through single-minded yoga and exclusive dedication;
likewise, resorting to solitary places, a fondness for secluded spots, and the abandonment of delight in the company of worldly folk.
The "internal" [knowledge] is that knowledge which resides within the self; its "perpetuity" is its state of being constantly contemplated.
Its "reality," however, is the Supreme Brahman, according to the Smṛti: "Those who know reality declare the reality to be the non-dual knowledge" (Bhagavad Gītā 13.12), and so forth.
The "vision" of the object of that knowledge—characterized by its attainment—is its recollection in the heart.

This [set of qualities] beginning with non-pride is declared to be knowledge (*jñāna*), as it is both a direct and an indirect means for the attainment of that [Self], according to the etymological derivation: "that by which one knows" (*jñāyate*) or "is perceived" (*upalabhyate*). That which is otherwise, being the opposite—namely pride and so forth—is ignorance (*ajñāna*), as it is contrary to the perception of that [Self]. //7–11//
I shall declare that which is to be known, by knowing which one attains immortality:
the beginningless Supreme Brahman, which is said to be neither existent nor non-existent. 13.12
Śrīdhara: With six verses beginning with "The Knowable" (jñeya), he describes that which is to be known by means of these aforementioned instruments.
He says, "I shall proclaim that which is to be known.
He demonstrates the fruit of knowledge in order to establish the listener's respect [for the teaching].
Having known that which is about to be described, one attains the immortal, which is liberation.
What is it? It is "without beginning" (*anādimat*);
because it does not have a beginning, it is "without beginning."
"Brahman" means the supreme, unsurpassed reality.

Although its state of being beginningless (*anādimattva*) is already established by the *bahuvrīhi* compound "beginningless" (*anādi*) alone, the further employment of the possessive suffix *-mat* is a Vedic (archaic) usage.
Alternatively, "anādi" and "mat-param" may be treated as two separate words.
The meaning is that my supreme, non-differentiated form of Viṣṇu is Brahman.

He states this very point: "It is neither being nor is it called non-being. That which is the object of a means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) through a positive formulation is expressed by the word "being" (sat).
The object of negation is expressed by the word "non-existent" (asat);
however, this [reality] is distinct from both of those, because it is not an object [of cognition]. This is the meaning. //12//
Madhusūdana:
In response to the expectation of what is to be known by means of these instruments denoted as "knowledge," he says, beginning with "That which is to be known" (jñeyaṃ yat tat), in six verses.
That which is to be known by one desiring liberation, that I shall proclaim—that is, I shall speak of it preeminently and with clarity.

In order to draw the listener’s attention, he speaks in praise by way of the fruit [of the teaching]: "Having known that which is to be known, as it will be described, one attains immortality—that is, one is liberated from saṃsāra.
What is that? It is the beginningless—that which has no beginning;
the supreme, unsurpassed Brahman, the reality of the Supreme Self, unconditioned in every respect.
In this context, although the meaning is already obtained by the bahuvrīhi compound *anādi* alone, the suffix *matup* is employed to express excellence or constant connection.
Furthermore, some maintain that the two words *anādi* and *mat-param* should be read together;
the meaning is that the Brahman which is beyond the qualified Brahman (*mat*) is the Brahman whose nature is devoid of attributes (*nirviśeṣa-rūpa*).
The interpretation that "I am the supreme power (parā śakti) of him who is called Vāsudeva" is a misinterpretation;
for since the subject to be established is Brahman devoid of distinctions, it is impossible to predicate the possession of power (śaktimattva) in that regard.
He states its very lack of distinction: "That is said to be neither existent nor non-existent.

The object of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) through the mode of affirmation is expressed by the word "existent" (*sat*); however, the object of a means of valid cognition through the mode of negation is expressed by the word "non-existent" (*asat*).

But this [Brahman] is distinct from both of those, because it is devoid of attributes and because its nature is self-luminous consciousness; for the Śruti says: "From whence words return, together with the mind, not having attained it" (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 2.4.1).
Therefore, that Brahman is not the locus of existence (*sadbhāva*).

Therefore, it cannot be expressed by any word in its primary sense (*mukhyayā vṛttyā*), because the grounds for the application of words (*śabda-pravṛtti-hetu*) are absent therein. For example, it is not [expressed] through genus (*jāti*), as in "cow" or "horse," nor through action (*kriyā*), as in "he cooks" or "he reads."
A word conveys its meaning either through qualities, as in "white" or "black," or through relations, as in "wealthy" or "possessing cows.

In this context, every property— whether distinct from action, quality, or relation, and whether of the nature of a universal (jāti) or a limiting adjunct (upādhi)— is subsumed under the term "universal" (jāti).

Even a proper name such as *Ḍittha* or *Ḍavittha* functions by taking some property—whether it be another entity or its own self—as the basis for its application; thus, it too is a genus-word (*jāti-śabda*).
Likewise, even the word "space" (*ākāśa*) functions among logicians by placing forward some property, such as being the substratum of sound.

In our own view, however, since individual instances of space (*ākāśa*)—which are produced like earth and other elements—are manifold, "spaciousness" (*ākāśatva*) is also indeed a universal (*jāti*); thus, that term too is a word denoting a universal.
Furthermore, there is no such thing as direction (*diś*) distinct from space, and time (*kāla*) is not distinct from the Lord (*īśvara*).

Alternatively, since even the words "direction" (dik) and "time" (kāla) function based on specific limiting adjuncts (upādhi) as their grounds for application, they too are indeed genus-words (jāti-śabda).
Therefore, because there are four kinds of grounds for application, word is of exactly four types.

In that context, the negation "it is neither existent nor non-existent" serves as an indicative mark (upalakṣaṇa) for the negation of action, quality, and relation as well, just as it is for the negation of the genus.
"Only one, without a second": this is the negation of *jāti* (universal), because it is impossible for that which subsists in multiple individuals to exist in a single one.
"Without qualities, without action, tranquil" [ŚvetU 6.19]: this is the sequential negation of the connection with qualities and actions.
"For this Puruṣa is indeed unattached."

And so it is said in [BAU 4.3.15]. Furthermore, there is the negation of everything in [BAU 2.3.6]: "Now, therefore, the instruction is 'not this, not this'. Therefore, it is logical that Brahman cannot be expressed by any word whatsoever.
If that is so, how is it that it was stated, "How shall I teach it? and how is the sūtra [VS 1.1.3], "Because it has the Śāstra as its source," to be understood?

Understand that it is communicated by the word through some manner of figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*). The method of this communication has been explained in the commentary on the verse, "Someone beholds him as a wonder" (Gītā 2.28);
the detailed account, however, is to be found in the *Bhāṣya*. //12//
Viśvanātha:
Thus, by means of these proofs, both the individual self (jīvātman) and the supreme self (paramātman) are to be known.
Among them, it is the supreme self alone that is all-pervading and is denoted by the term "Brahman."
And that Brahman, both without attributes (*nirviśeṣa*) and with attributes (*saviśeṣa*), is to be meditated upon respectively by the man of knowledge (*jñānin*) and the devotee (*bhakta*).
Even when residing within the body, it is to be contemplated as having four arms and is designated by the term "Supreme Self" (*paramātman*).
In this regard, he first states that Brahman is the object of knowledge (*jñeya*).
"Without beginning" means that which has no beginning; the sense is that it is eternal because its nature is identical to mine.
"Having Me as the Supreme" means that I alone am its supreme and most excellent support, as I have previously stated: "For I am the foundation of Brahman" (Gītā 14.27).
In response to the inquiry "What is that?", he says:
That Brahman is neither existent nor non-existent; the meaning is that it transcends both cause and effect. //12//
Baladeva: Having thus taught the means of knowledge, he now teaches that which is to be known by those means in the verse beginning with "That which is to be known.

That object of knowledge to be apprehended through the aforementioned means—the reality of the individual self (jīvātman)—I shall explain clearly and with ease, so that by knowing it, a person attains or gains immortality, which is liberation (mokṣa).
In this regard, he teaches the reality of the individual self with the half-verse beginning with "beginningless" (anādi).
That which has no beginning is that for which there is no initial birth of the individual soul (*jīva*); therefore, because it does not arise, it is eternal—this is the meaning.
Thus says the Śruti: "The wise one is neither born nor dies" (KaṭhU 1.2.18), and so forth.
He is the Lord of the Pradhāna and the Knower of the Field (*kṣetrajña*), the Master of the Guṇas, according to the Śruti: "I alone am the supreme Lord" (ŚvetU 6.16).

And because of the traditional teaching (smṛti) that "He is the servant of Hari alone, never of anyone else," [the Self] is distinguished by the eightfold qualities of Brahman, such as being free from sin (apahatapāpman). And the Śruti says thus: "That Self which is free from sin, ageless, deathless, sorrowless, free from hunger and thirst, whose resolve is true—that is what is to be sought, that is what is to be desired to be known."

Thus, the word "Brahman" refers to the individual soul (*jīva*) based on such scriptural passages as, "If one knows Brahman as consciousness" (*Taittirīya Upaniṣad* 2.5.1), and from what will be stated later:
"Having transcended these qualities, he is fit for becoming Brahman" (*Gītā* 14.26); and "Having become Brahman, with a serene self, he neither grieves nor desires" (*Gītā* 18.55).
That pure reality of the individual self (*jīvātman*) is not called "existent" because it is devoid of the two states consisting of cause and effect; nor is it called "non-existent.

Rather, it is described as the consciousness of the atom (*paramāṇu-caitanya*) characterized by the eightfold qualities (*guṇāṣṭaka*). The meaning is that it is called "existent" when in the state of effect, with name and form differentiated (*vibhakta-nāma-rūpa*), and "non-existent" when in the state of cause, with name and form dissolved (*upamṛdita-nāma-rūpa*). (BhG 13.13)
With hands and feet everywhere, with eyes, heads, and faces everywhere, possessing ears everywhere in the world, it stands pervading everything. 13.

Śrīdhara: Now, one might object that if Brahman is thus distinct from both the existent and the non-existent, it would contradict such scriptural passages as "All this, indeed, is Brahman" and "All this is Brahman alone. Anticipating this, [the author] states that through its inconceivable power—well-known from scriptures such as "Its power is declared to be manifold, and its knowledge, strength, and action are inherent"—Brahman possesses the nature of being the Self of all.

Showing this to him, he says with five verses beginning with "sarvataḥ": that [body] which has hands and feet everywhere— that is, on all sides— and which has eyes, heads, and mouths everywhere— that is, on all sides.
Possessing ears everywhere, that is, endowed with the sense of hearing in all places, it exists pervading and encompassing everything in the world;
the meaning is that it exists as the locus of all worldly transactions through the limiting adjuncts (upādhi) such as hands and so forth, which constitute the functions of all living beings. //13//
Madhusūdana:

Thus, although the suspicion that Brahman— which is devoid of limiting adjuncts— is non-existent has been dispelled by the statement "it is not non-existent" because it is not an object of the word or cognition "being," nevertheless, for the sake of removing that suspicion in detail, [the Lord speaks] by means of the limiting adjuncts of the organs of all living beings.
Establishing its existence by way of its nature as the conscious Knower of the Field (*kṣetrajña*), he says "from everywhere" (*sarvataḥ*).

From everywhere—in all bodies—the hands and feet are insentient and must be set in motion toward their respective functions by the conscious Knower of the Field. Therefore, that [Knower] is to be known as having hands and feet everywhere, because all activities of the insentient are preceded by the presiding of a conscious principle. Since that conscious Brahman, the Knower of the Field, is the cause of the activity of the entire aggregate of the insentient, there is no room for doubt regarding its non-existence.
The meaning is as follows:
"Having eyes, heads, and mouths on all sides" refers to that in which eyes, heads, and mouths are to be manifested everywhere.
Likewise, "having ears on all sides" refers to that in which auditory faculties (śrutayaḥ) are to be manifested as existing everywhere.

In the world, within the entire collection of living beings, [the Self] alone remains as the one, eternal, and all-pervading, having overspread and permeated the entire insentient category by its own existence and manifestation through an adventitious relation; it attains a state of being entirely changeless.
The meaning is that it does not become connected, even in the slightest degree, with the defects or qualities of the insentient phenomenal world superimposed upon it—just as, for example:
And in all bodies, there is only one single consciousness, which is eternal and omnipresent, not distinct for each body; this has been explained previously. //13//
Viśvanātha:
