Now, one might object that if Brahman is thus distinct from both the existent and the non-existent, it would contradict such scriptural passages as "All this, indeed, is Brahman" and "All this is Brahman alone. Anticipating this, [the author states that] although [Brahman] by its very nature transcends cause and effect, [there remains the relationship] between power (*śakti*) and the possessor of power (*śaktimān*).
Because there is no difference [between them], He is also of the nature of cause and effect; thus he says: "That from which hands and feet extend in every direction.
The meaning is that since the multitudes of hands and feet belonging to all beings, from Brahmā down to the smallest ant, are seen everywhere, that Brahman is endowed with innumerable hands and feet.
In the same way, "eyes in every direction," and so forth. (13)
Baladeva: Now, [the Lord] teaches the reality of the Supreme Self with the verse beginning "hands and feet everywhere.
That reality of the Supreme Self has hands and feet everywhere, and so forth; the meaning is clear. (13)
It appears to possess the qualities of all the senses, yet it is devoid of all senses; it is unattached and yet the sustainer of all, devoid of qualities and yet the experiencer of qualities. //14//
Śrīdhara: Furthermore, regarding the phrase "by all the senses" (*sarvendriya*):
it appears in the form of each respective [object] within the functions (*vṛtti*) of all the senses, such as the eyes, which consist of the qualities (*guṇa*) such as color-form (*rūpa*).
Alternatively, it causes all the senses, the qualities, and their respective objects to appear.
And it is devoid of all sense organs;
likewise, the Śruti says: "Without hands or feet, he is swift and a grasper; he sees without eyes, he hears without ears," and so forth.
It is unattached, meaning free from attachment.
Nevertheless, because it sustains everything, it is the substratum of all.
That very same [Self] is *nirguṇa*, meaning devoid of the qualities such as *sattva* and the rest;
yet it is also the *guṇa-bhoktṛ*, the experiencer and protector of the qualities, namely *sattva* and the others. //14//
Madhusūdana:

Following the maxim that "the non-differentiated is explained through superimposition and negation," it was previously explained that the beginningless Supreme Brahman exists by means of the superimposition of the entire phenomenal world; now, by means of its negation, it is explained that "it is said to be neither existent nor non-existent."
One undertakes with all the senses for the sake of knowing the nature of the Self as free from limiting adjuncts (*nirupādhi*).

In reality, that [Self] is devoid of all senses; yet through its illusory power (*māyā*), it appears to possess the qualities of all the senses—namely, by means of the functions of determination (*adhyavasāya*), volition (*saṅkalpa*), hearing, speaking, and so forth, which belong to all the external organs such as the ear, as well as the two internal organs, the intellect (*buddhi*) and the mind (*manas*).

That Knowable Brahman appears as if having the form of each respective object and as if engaged in the operations of all the senses; for the Śruti says: "It meditates, as it were, and moves, as it were" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.3.7).
Here, "meditation" is an indicative mark for the operation of the cognitive senses.
"Leaving" (*lelāyana*) means moving; it is intended as an illustration of the activity of the organs of action (*karmendriya*).
Likewise, from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārtha*), it is unattached and indeed devoid of all connections;
yet, through illusion (*māyā*), it sustains everything and, by its nature as Being (*sat*), it appears to maintain and nourish all that is imagined—thus it is "the sustainer of all."
Because an error without a substratum is impossible;
likewise, in the ultimate sense, it is devoid of qualities (*nirguṇa*), meaning it is indeed free from the qualities of *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas*.

And it is the "experiencer of the qualities" (*guṇa-bhoktṛ*), meaning that which experiences—that is, perceives—the qualities of *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas* as they transform into the forms of pleasure, pain, and delusion through the medium of sound and the other sense objects; this is the meaning of that Knowable Brahman.
Viśvanātha:
Furthermore, because it illuminates all the senses, the qualities, and the objects of the senses, it is called "the eye of the eye," according to such scriptural passages (*śruti*).
Alternatively, it is that which shines forth and manifests through all the senses and their qualities, such as sound and the rest.
That [Self] is also devoid of all sense organs, being free from ordinary organs and the like.
Thus says the Śruti: "Without hands or feet, He is swift and a grasper; He sees without eyes, He hears without ears," and so forth.
The meaning is that He is the locus of the powers well-known through the Śruti, which states: "His supreme power is indeed heard to be manifold, consisting of innate knowledge, strength, and action."
Unattached, meaning devoid of attachment; the sustainer of all, protecting everything in His form as the glorious Viṣṇu;
Nirguṇa, whose nature is free from the qualities such as *sattva* and the rest;
furthermore, the enjoyer of the qualities (*guṇa-bhoktṛ*), who tastes the six divine attributes denoted by the word *Bhaga*, transcending the three *guṇas*. //14//
Baladeva: Furthermore, regarding the word "sarva" (all): it shines or blazes by means of all the senses and their qualities—that is, their functions—and thus [the Lord] is so described.

It must be accepted that Hari is devoid of and abandoned by all the senses—which, like the vital breaths (*jīvendriya*), are distinct from His essential nature—and is empty of material instruments, yet is distinguished by those [senses] which are inseparable from His own nature.

"Without hands or feet, he is swift and a grasper; without eyes, he sees; without ears, he hears. Of what nature is the Blessed One? Of that same nature is his manifestation. Of what nature is the Blessed One? He is of the nature of knowledge (*jñāna*), of the nature of sovereignty (*aiśvarya*), and of the nature of power (*śakti*). We perceive the Blessed One as possessing intellect, mind, limbs, and minor members; he is possessed of intellect.

According to the scripture, "He possesses the mind, the arrows, and the limbs of the body," [the Self] is the sustainer of all, the upholder of all principles (*tattva*), yet remains unattached because it upholds them through mere volition (*saṅkalpa*) alone, being devoid of contact with them. It is without qualities (*nirguṇa*), for the scripture states: "The witness, the cognizer, absolute and without qualities. Thus, although touched by the qualities of *māyā*, it is the enjoyer of the qualities of existence by virtue of being the controller.
Beginning with "Ignorance (ajñā) is the producer of transformations that experience the qualities," [it continues] up to "But the one God drinks alone."
Here, the Lord, the all-pervading one, by means of meditation and action, forcibly enjoys those who follow his will according to his own desire.
Because it is so stated in scripture. //14//
It exists both outside and within all beings, as the unmoving and indeed as the moving;
because of its subtlety, it is incomprehensible; it is far away, and yet it is near.
Śrīdhara: Furthermore, regarding the word "outside" (*bahiḥ*):
that very [Brahman] exists both outside and inside all beings—both moving and non-moving—which are its own effects, just as gold exists in bracelets, earrings, and so forth;
and just as water exists both inside and outside the waves of water.
The entire range of beings— whether stationary (sthāvara) or moving (cara), whether immobile or mobile— is that very [Brahman] alone,
because the effect has the cause as its essence.

Nevertheless, due to its subtlety and its being devoid of form and other such qualities, it is not clearly recognizable as "this is that," and thus it does not become an object fit for explicit knowledge.
For this very reason, for the ignorant, it is as if situated at a distance, separated by hundreds of thousands of yojanas,
because it is beyond the *prakṛti* which is subject to modification;
but for the wise, on the contrary, because it is their own inner self (*pratyag-ātman*), it is near and eternally present.
And so says the mantra:
"That moves; that moves not.
That is far away; that is near."
It is within all this,
and it is outside of all this.
[Īśopaniṣad 5] Thus:
"It moves, it stirs; it does not move, it does not stir.
The phrase "tad u antike" (that indeed is near) is the division [of the verse]. //15//
Madhusūdana:

[The term] *bhūtānām* means of all things characterized by coming into being; [the term] *adhiṣṭhānam* means the one unimagined substrate of all imagined effects. The meaning is that, like a rope [is the substrate] of the imagined snake, stream of water, and so forth, it pervades everything in its entirety, both externally and internally.
For this very reason, the entire collection of beings—both the stationary (sthāvara) and the moving (jaṅgama)—is that very [Brahman], because its nature is the substratum (adhiṣṭhāna).
The meaning is that nothing among imagined things is distinct from it.

Thus, although it is the self of all, because of its subtlety and its lack of form and other qualities, it cannot be known as "this is such-and-such" and does not become an object for clear cognition.

For this very reason, because it is unattainable even in ten million billion years for those devoid of the means for self-knowledge, it is "far away," as if separated by hundreds of thousands of millions of *yojanas*.
But for those endowed with the means for knowledge, it is "near," being not at all remote since it is one's very Self.
This is according to such scriptural passages as: "Farther than the far, yet here near to those who see; it is placed right here within the cave of the heart" (*Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad* 3.1.7). //15//
Viśvanātha:
Just as space and so forth exist both outside and inside living beings— that is, their own effects— such as bodies,
the entire collection of beings, whether immobile (sthāvara) or mobile (jaṅgama), is that very same [Brahman].
Because the effect is of the nature of its cause;
even so, because it is distinct from form and the other [sensory objects], it cannot be clearly known as "this is that" and thus is not fit for clear cognition.
For this very reason, it stands as far away as ten million leagues to the ignorant, yet to the wise, it is situated right at home, in their very presence.

And because it is the inner controller (antaryāmin) within one's own body, it is "farther than the far" yet "near here" even while being seen; for this is established by such scriptural passages as, "It is hidden right here in the cave of the heart" (Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 3.1.7). //15//

Baladeva: "Outside" means that He exists both outside and inside all beings—the principles (tattvas) consisting of both the conscious and the insentient—because of the scriptural revelation: "Pervading all that is within and without, Nārāyaṇa stands" (MNU 13.5).
According to the Śruti: "The unmoving moves, and the moving is unmoving; seated, it goes far; lying down, it travels everywhere" (KaṭhU 1.2.21).
Because of its subtlety, its nature as the inner self (*pratyak*), and its form being consciousness-bliss (*cit-sukha*), it is unknowable—it cannot be known like other deities.
Therefore, it is "situated afar," for the Śruti says: "No one perceives it with the mind, nor does anyone see it with the eye" (ŚvetU 4.20).
"But by means of an organ [of perception] permeated by devotion—just as the ear is permeated by music—that [Reality] can be known," thus he says: "And that is near.
It should be viewed as being within the mind itself; for a certain wise person beheld the inner Self (pratyag-ātman).

For this is established by such scriptural passages as "Indeed, he abides in bhakti-yoga" (GTU 2.78), and by such traditional texts as "But by unswerving devotion He can be known" (Gītā 11.55). //15//
And that which is to be known is undivided among beings, yet appears as if divided; it is the sustainer of beings, the devourer, and the source of their manifestation. 16.16
Śrīdhara: Furthermore, regarding the phrase "undivided" (*avibhaktam*):

within all beings—consisting of both the stationary and the moving—it is undivided as the nature of the cause (*kāraṇātmanā*), yet it exists as if divided, being distinct as the nature of the effect (*kāryātmanā*). Just as foam and other such things born from the ocean do not become something other than the ocean, [so too is this].
Its very nature has been described as that which is to be known, the sustainer and nourisher of beings during the period of maintenance;
at the time of dissolution, it is "devouring," having the habit of consuming; and at the time of creation, it is "procreative," having the habit of manifesting itself through various effects. //16//
Madhusūdana:
He explains what was stated—that it alone exists pervading everything—in order to refute those who maintain that the self is divided in each body, by using the term "undivided" (*avibhaktam*).
Within all beings, that is to say, within all living creatures, it is undivided, non-different, and indeed one.
However, it is not divided according to each body, because it is all-pervasive like space.
Nevertheless, because it is perceived through identification with the body, it exists as if partitioned for each body.
The meaning is that, due to its being adventitious, the appearance of difference therein is unreal, just as in the case of space.

[Objection: Let it be that the *kṣetrajña* (the knower of the field) is one and all-pervading; however, Brahman, the cause of the world, must be distinct from that. [Reply: No; for He is the sustainer of beings (*bhūtabhartṛ*), meaning He sustains all beings during the time of their maintenance; likewise, at the time of dissolution He is *grasiṣṇu*, having the nature of devouring, and at the time of creation He is *prabhaviṣṇu*, having the nature of bringing forth.

Of everything, just as a rope and the like are the cause of a snake and so forth imagined through illusion; therefore, that Brahman which is the cause of the world’s maintenance, dissolution, and origination is alone to be known as the Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña), one and the same in every body, and not anything other than that—this is the meaning. //16//
Viśvanātha:

Within all beings—consisting of both the stationary and the moving—that very essence which is Śrī Nārāyaṇa is undivided as the causal self (remaining non-different), yet it exists as if divided and distinct as the effected self. That alone is the Reality.
The sustainer of beings during the period of their existence; the protector; the devourer at the time of dissolution, that is, the destroyer;
and the powerful one at the time of creation, whose nature is to manifest as various effects. //16//

Baladeva: "Undivided" means that within the individual souls (*jīvas*), which are divided and mutually distinct, that one Brahman remains undivided, yet appears as if divided and distinct for each soul, according to the Vedic scripture: "Being one, it is seen as manifold."
Viṣṇu alone is the supreme one everywhere; of this there is no doubt.
Due to his sovereignty, he possesses a single form.
Like the sun, it is manifested in many ways.
And because of this traditional teaching (smṛti):
"And that [Self] is the sustainer of beings during their existence, the protector of beings; at dissolution, it is the devourer, the destroyer by means of the power of Time;
and at creation, it is the source of manifestation, having the nature of manifesting as various effects through the powers of Pradhāna and the individual soul."

And the Śruti says: "That from which these beings are born, that by which, once born, they live, and into which they enter at their departure—that is Brahman; seek to know that" (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 3.1.1). //16//
That is said to be the light even of lights, beyond darkness;
it is knowledge, the object of knowledge, and the goal of knowledge, established in the hearts of all. 13.17
Śrīdhara: Furthermore, regarding the phrase "even of lights":
it is the light that illuminates even the lights, such as the sun and others;
by which [light] the sun shines, kindled by its splendor.
There the sun does not shine, nor do the moon and the stars;
these lightnings do not shine, much less this fire. That alone shines, and everything shines after it.
By its light all this shines.
This is according to such scriptural passages as [KaṭhU 2.5.15].
For this very reason, He is said to be "beyond darkness," meaning untouched by ignorance (ajñāna),
based on scriptural passages such as "of solar hue, beyond the darkness" [ŚvetU 3.8].
And that very knowledge is manifested in the modification (vṛtti) of the intellect;
it is both the object of knowledge (jñeya), appearing in the form of color and so forth, and that which is accessible to knowledge.
The meaning is that it is to be attained by means of the previously mentioned instruments of knowledge characterized by humility and the like.
He distinguishes [the Self] as that which is attainable through knowledge, situated in the heart of every living being, specifically abiding as the controller with its own nature unshaken.
In the reading *dhiṣṭhitam*, the meaning is "having presided over" (*adhiṣṭhāya*) while remaining.
— Madhusūdana.

[Objection: "If that [Brahman], though existing everywhere, is not perceived, then it must indeed be insentient (jaḍa). It cannot be self-luminous (svayaṃjyotis), for even if it were, its being ungraspable by the senses and so forth would be established simply because it is devoid of form and other such qualities. To this he says: "Of lights" (jyotiṣām).

That Knowable, Brahman, is the light of the illuminators—such as the sun and others, as well as the intellect and so forth, both external and internal—and it is the illuminator itself; for it is logical that a light distinct from these [others] should be the illuminator of insentient lights.
And because of such scriptural passages as, "By whose splendor the sun shines, kindled with brilliance; by his light all this vibrantly shines" (KaṭhU 2.5.15),
and because he will say later, "The splendor that resides in the sun" (Gītā 15.12), and so forth.

Even though [the Self] is not inherently insentient (*jaḍa*), one might think it could become associated with the insentient; to this he says "no. It is beyond the category of the insentient (*tamaso jaḍa-vargāt param*), untouched by ignorance (*avidyā*) and its effects, which are both non-ultimate (*apāramārthika*); that Brahman is ultimate (*pāramārthika*) because a relationship between the existent and the non-existent is impossible.

This is stated in such scriptural passages as "Higher than the Imperishable is the High" (*akṣarāt parataḥ paraḥ*), and so forth, as well as by the proponents of Brahman (*brahma-vādibhiḥ*). As it has been said:
A real union between the Self— which is unattached and immutable— and the non-Self— which is characterized by attachment and subject to change— is not possible.
And from the Vedic scripture: "Of solar hue, beyond darkness.
The phrase "of solar hue" means that in its own manifestation it does not depend on any other light, but is the illuminator of all.

Since it is self-luminous and untouched by insentience (*jaḍa*), for that very reason that knowledge consists of the nature of consciousness (*saṃvit*) manifested through a mental modification (*ceto-vṛtti*) produced by a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).

For this very reason, that alone is worthy of being known (*jñeyam*), because it is unknown; for that which is insentient (*jaḍa*) is not worthy of being known, as it lacks the state of being unknown.

How then is it not known by all? To this he says: "attainable through knowledge" (*jñāna-gamyam*). This means it is to be reached or attained through the previously mentioned collection of means—beginning with humility (*amānitvam*) and ending with the vision of the goal of the knowledge of reality (*tattva-jñānārtha-darśanam*)—which, being the cause of knowledge, is designated by the word "knowledge," but not without that.
Now, if it is to be reached through spiritual practice (*sādhana*), is it then separated by another place?
No; he says: "It is seated in the heart of all. It is seated in the heart—that is, in the intellect (*buddhi*)—of every class of living beings.
Although it exists everywhere in a general sense, it is seated there in a specific form, manifested as the individual soul (*jīva*) and as the inner controller (*antaryāmin*).

The meaning is that, like solar radiance in a mirror, a sun-stone, or similar objects, it is in fact unobstructed; yet, due to delusion, it appears as if obstructed, and through the cessation of ignorance—the cause of all error—it is as if attained. //17//
Viśvanātha: That light is the illuminator even of the luminaries— the moon and the sun—
by which the sun shines, kindled by its splendor.
There the sun does not shine, nor do the moon and the stars; these lightnings do not shine, much less this earthly fire. It is that alone which shines, and everything else shines after it.
By its light, all this shines forth.
This is according to such scriptural passages as [KaṭhU 2.5.15].
For this very reason, He is said to be beyond darkness— that is, beyond ignorance— and untouched by it,
according to such scriptural passages as "Having the color of the sun, beyond the darkness" (ŚvetU 3.8).

That very [consciousness], when manifested in the modification of the intellect (*buddhi-vṛtti*), is called "knowledge" (*jñāna*). That same [consciousness], having transformed into the form of color and so forth, is the "knowable" (*jñeya*).

The meaning is that this very [consciousness] is "attainable through knowledge," i.e., to be reached by means of the previously mentioned instruments of knowledge such as humility (*amānitva*) and the rest.
The meaning is that this very nature of the Supreme Self, being real, abides as the presiding controller, established within the heart of every living being. //17//
Baladeva: That Brahman is the light that illumines even the luminaries, such as the sun;
"There the sun does not shine, nor the moon or the stars, nor do these lightnings shine, much less this fire."
"That alone shines; everything else shines after it; by its light all this is illumined"—from such scriptural passages as these, that is Brahman.
That Brahman is said to be beyond the darkness of primordial nature (*prakṛti*) and untouched by it, according to the Śruti: "The sun-colored one, beyond the darkness" (ŚvetU 3.8).
Knowledge is said to have consciousness as its sole essence, according to the Śruti: "Knowledge is Brahman, a mass of bliss" (GTU 2.79).

Knowledge is said to be worthy of being known as the refuge for one seeking liberation, according to the Śruti: "I, the seeker of liberation, indeed take refuge in that God who is the light of the intellect" (GTU 1.25).
It is said to be "attainable through knowledge" according to the Śruti: "Having known Him alone, one transcends death" (ŚvetU 3.8).

It is said to be "established in the heart of every living being" as its controller, abiding by presiding over it, according to the Śruti: "He has entered within, the ruler of people" (TaittĀ 3.11.10). Nor should the pentad beginning with "hands on all sides" be interpreted as referring solely to the individual soul (jīva), because of the context and other reasons; for the Lord (Īśvara) is also the subject under discussion as the Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña), just like the individual soul.

Because the Śvetāśvataras, having commenced with Brahman itself, recite the passage beginning with "sarvataḥ pāṇi" (ŚvetU 3.16) along with its supplement, and because inconsistency within the context is observed throughout the Upaniṣads. //17//
Thus, the field, as well as knowledge and the object of knowledge, have been described in brief.
My devotee, having realized this, attains to my own state of being. (13.18)
Śrīdhara: He concludes the discussion on the field (*kṣetra*) and so forth, along with the qualified person (*adhikārin*) and the fruit (*phala*), with the words "Thus" (*iti*).
Thus, this field consists of everything from the great elements (*mahābhūta*) down to fortitude (*dhṛti*);
likewise, knowledge (*jñāna*) consists of everything from humility (*amānitva*) up to the vision of the purpose of the knowledge of reality (*tattvajñānārthadarśana*).

And that which is to be known—the supreme Brahman without beginning, and so forth, ending with "it is established"—has been described at length by Vasiṣṭha and others; all of that has been stated by me here in brief. And how is this so?
My devotee, possessing the characteristics described in the preceding chapter, having realized My state, becomes fit—that is, capable—for attaining Brahmanhood. //18//
Madhusūdana:
Having spoken of the field and so forth, He concludes by stating the qualified seeker and the fruit with the words "thus" (*iti*).
By this aforementioned manner, the field consists of everything from the great elements (*mahābhūta*) up to fortitude (*dhṛti*).
Likewise, knowledge— beginning with humility (*amānitva*) and ending with the vision of the reality that is the goal of knowledge—

and the object of knowledge— the beginningless, supreme Brahman who is established [as the source]— have all been drawn from the Śrutis and Smṛtis and briefly stated by me for the benefit of those of dull intellect.
For this much alone constitutes the entirety of the meaning of the Vedas and the meaning of the Gītā.

And he states that only my devotee, possessing the characteristics described in the preceding chapter, is qualified for this: "My devotee"— one who has surrendered his entire being to me, the Blessed Lord Vāsudeva, the supreme teacher, and who takes refuge in me alone— "having discerned," that is, having understood through discrimination, "this" aforementioned field, knowledge, and the object of knowledge, [strives] "for my state," which is the state of supreme bliss free from all misfortune.
He becomes fit for liberation; he becomes capable of attaining liberation.
For that high-souled one who has supreme devotion for the Divine, and as for the Divine, so for the Guru—for him these truths that have been declared shine forth clearly.
Thus says the Śruti.

Therefore, the intention is as Viśvanātha states: "Desiring the supreme goal of human life, one who has always taken refuge in Me alone should pursue only the means for the knowledge of the Self, having abandoned the craving for the enjoyment of trivial objects."
He concludes the discussion on the field and so forth, along with the qualified practitioner and the fruit, by saying "thus":
the field consists of the great elements and so on, ending with fortitude;
knowledge consists of humility and so on, ending with the vision of the meaning of the reality of things.

From "the object of knowledge, attainable through wisdom, and beginningless" up to "established," the single reality— Brahman, which is denoted by the terms Bhagavat and Paramātman— has been stated in brief. My devotee, the one possessed of devotion and the one possessed of knowledge, [strives] for my state, that is, for union with me (*mat-sāyujya*).

Or rather, my single-minded devotee, being my servant, having realized this—that "this is the extent of the sovereignty of me, my Lord"—becomes fit for, that is, endowed with, devotion (bhāva), which is love, toward me. //18//

Baladeva: He concludes what has been stated regarding the field (*kṣetra*) and so forth, together with the fruit of its knowledge, with the words "Thus the field" (*iti kṣetram*). From "the great elements" (*mahābhūtāni*) up to "consciousness and fortitude" (*cetanā dhṛtiḥ*), the nature of the field has been described.

From "humility" (*amānitvam*) up to "the vision of the purpose of the knowledge of reality" (*tattvajñānārthadarśanam*), the knowledge of the two knowable fields and the means for that [knowledge] have been described.
By the passage beginning with "without beginning, having Me as the supreme" and ending with "seated in the heart of all," I have described the two types of the Knowable and the Knower.

Having understood these three through their mutual distinction, my devotee becomes fit—that is, capable—for attaining My state, which is either My love or My own nature, and for liberation from transmigratory existence. //18//
Know that both Prakṛti and Puruṣa are indeed beginningless;
know also that the modifications and the qualities (guṇas) arise from Prakṛti. 13.19
Śrīdhara: Thus far, it has been explained what that field is and of what nature it is.

Now, however, he elaborates—by means of five verses beginning with "prakṛtim"—upon that which was previously promised: what undergoes modification, from what [cause] it arises, who [the agent] is, and what his power is; this by way of explaining how Prakṛti and Puruṣa are the causes of transmigratory existence.
In that regard, if Prakṛti and Puruṣa were to have a beginning, then those two would also require another Prakṛti, which would result in an infinite regress.
Therefore, know that both of them are without beginning;
for Prakṛti is without beginning because she is the power (śakti) of the beginningless Lord.
Since the individual soul (*puruṣa*) is also a portion of that [Supreme Self], it too is indeed beginningless.

Furthermore, the fact that the Supreme Lord and His powers are beginningless and eternal has been established by the venerable author of the *Śaṅkarabhāṣya* through extensive treatises; therefore, we shall not elaborate upon it here for fear of excessive prolixity.

Know that the modifications—such as the body, the senses, and so forth—and the qualities—such as pleasure, pain, and delusion, which are transformations of the *guṇas*—have all arisen from *prakṛti*. //19//
Madhusūdana:
By this text, that which is the field (*kṣetra*) and what its nature is have been explained.
Now, that which undergoes modification, from whence it arises, who He is, and what His power is—this much remains to be explained.

In this context, by explaining how *prakṛti* (primordial nature) and *puruṣa* (the spirit) are the causes of *saṃsāra*, the verse beginning with "That which changes, from which [it arises], and that [which is the cause]" (*yad vikāri yataś ca yat*)—referring to *prakṛti*—is elaborated through two verses; whereas the verse beginning with "And he who, and what his power is" (*sa ca yo yat-prabhāvaś ca*)—referring to *puruṣa*—is elaborated through two [other] verses. This is the distinction.

Therein, in the seventh chapter, having presented the two natures of the Lord—the higher and the lower, characterized as the *kṣetra* (field) and the *kṣetrajña* (knower of the field)—it was stated: "All beings have this as their source" (*etad-yonīni bhūtāni*).

In this regard, having stated that the lower *prakṛti* is characterized as the field (*kṣetra*) while the higher is characterized as the living being (*jīva*), and thus both are beginningless, it is now said that all beings have these two as their source in the verse beginning with "prakṛtim.
*Prakṛti* is the power of the Supreme Lord called *māyā*, consisting of the three *guṇas*, which was previously described as the lower *prakṛti* characterized as the field.

That which was previously called the higher *prakṛti* and designated as the living being (*jīva*) is here referred to as the *puruṣa*; thus, there is no contradiction between what precedes and what follows.
Know that both Prakṛti and Puruṣa are indeed beginningless— that is,
they have no beginning or cause.
Likewise, the beginninglessness of Prakṛti is due to its being the cause of the entire universe.
If that [agency] were also dependent on a cause, it would lead to the consequence of an infinite regress.
Therefore, the person (puruṣa) is beginningless, because the entire world is impelled by his merit and demerit, as evidenced by the occurrence of joy, sorrow, and fear in all born beings;
otherwise, there would be the consequence of the loss of what was done and the acquisition of what was not done.

Since Prakṛti is beginningless, its being the source of the elements mentioned previously is logical; thus he says: "And the sixteen modifications—the five great elements and the eleven senses—and the qualities consisting of sattva, rajas, and tamas, which are pleasure, pain, and delusion, are indeed born from Prakṛti alone."
Know, that is, understand, them to be caused by primordial nature alone. //19//
Viśvanātha:

Having spoken of the Supreme Self, in response to the inquiry as to how the individual self—the one denoted by the term *kṣetrajña*—can have contact with *māyā*, and when that commencement occurred, he says: "Know both *prakṛti* (māyā) and *puruṣa* (the individual self) to be beginningless (*anādī*)," meaning those for whom no beginning or cause exists. Because they are beginningless...
Because they are my power, as I am the Lord:
"Earth, water, fire, air, ether, mind, intellect,
and ego— thus is this nature of mine divided eightfold."
"Know that this nature of Mine is inferior; but know My other, higher nature, O mighty-armed one, which is the soul-nature by which this world is sustained" (Gītā 7.5).
From this statement of Mine, the meaning is that since both Māyā and the individual soul (jīva) are My powers and are therefore beginningless, their conjunction as well is beginningless.
In this regard, he says that although these two are mutually conjoined, they are indeed distinct in reality:

"Know the modifications—such as the body, the senses, and so forth—and the qualities—the transformations of the *guṇas* such as pleasure, pain, grief, and delusion—to have arisen from *prakṛti*, to have originated from *prakṛti*. Thus, he indicates that the individual soul (*jīva*) is indeed distinct from *prakṛti*, which has transformed into the form of the field (*kṣetra*).
The meaning is: "Know this. //19//

Baladeva: Thus, by the verses beginning with "prakṛtim," the beginningless nature of the association between primordial material nature (prakṛti) and the individual soul (jīva)—which are mutually distinct by nature and both beginningless—is described, as well as the differentiation of their effects when conjoined, and the cause of that beginningless association. The particle *api* is used in the sense of emphasis (*avadhṛtau*).

Know that both Prakṛti and Puruṣa are joined together from time immemorial; know them to be indeed eternal because they are My powers (śakti). Their status as My powers has already been stated previously in such passages as "Earth, water... and so forth.

With the intention of showing that there is a distinction between their essential natures even though they have been joined since beginningless time, [the Lord] says: "transformations such as the body, senses, and so forth."

"Know that the qualities, as well as pleasure and pain, are born of *prakṛti*, are material (*prākṛta*), and not individual (*jaiva*). By this it is shown that the *jīva* is distinct from *prakṛti* as it has been transformed into the form of the field (*kṣetra*). //19//
In the matter of being the agent of effects and causes, Prakṛti is said to be the cause;
in the matter of being the experiencer of pleasures and pains, Puruṣa is said to be the cause. //20//

Śrīdhara: Demonstrating that modifications arise from primordial nature (prakṛti), he shows that the person (puruṣa) is the cause of transmigratory existence by means of the verse beginning with "kārya.
"Kārya" refers to the body;
"kāraṇāni" refers to the senses, which are the instruments for pleasure and pain.
Regarding their agency—that is, the transformation into those specific forms—Prakṛti is said by Kapila and others to be the cause.
The Puruṣa, however, the individual soul, is said to be the cause for the experience of the pleasure and pain produced therein.
The meaning is this: although agency does not naturally belong to the insentient Prakṛti, likewise, the capacity for experience does not belong to the unchanging Puruṣa.
Nevertheless, so-called agency (kartṛtva) consists in being the accomplisher of an action.

And that is possible even for an insentient thing because it is presided over by consciousness through the power of the unseen merit/demerit (adṛṣṭa) of a conscious being; as, for example, the upward flaming of fire, the horizontal movement of the wind, and the flowing of the milk from a cow's udder due to the power of the calf’s unseen merit, and so forth.

Therefore, due to the proximity of the Puruṣa, agency is attributed to Prakṛti, as well as the state of being an enjoyer—the experience of pleasure and pain—and since that [experience] is indeed an attribute of consciousness, the state of being an enjoyer is attributed to the Puruṣa due to the proximity of Prakṛti. //20//

Madhusūdana, analyzing how modifications arise from primordial nature (*prakṛti*), demonstrates that the person (*puruṣa*) is the cause of transmigratory existence (*saṃsāra*) through the verse beginning with "kārya.

Here, the term "kārya" (effect) includes the body, the instruments which are the senses, the thirteen elements residing therein that initiate the body, and the objects of the senses. All these are subsumed under the category of "effect" in this context.

The qualities (guṇas), consisting of pleasure, pain, and delusion, are included under the term "instrument" (karaṇa) because they reside in the instruments; thus, by the mention of the instrument, they are grasped.
Prakṛti is called the cause—the instrumental cause—for the agency of those effects and instruments, that is, for their transformation into those respective forms.
This remains the same meaning even when the reading is "kārya-karaṇa" with a long vowel.

Having thus explained that *prakṛti* is the cause of *saṃsāra*, he now states what the nature of the *puruṣa* is in that regard: "The *puruṣa* is the knower of the field (*kṣetrajña*), the supreme *prakṛti*," as was explained previously.

He is said to be the cause for the experience of all objects of enjoyment—namely, pleasure, pain, and delusion—insofar as he is the enjoyer (*bhoktṛ*) through the apprehension [of objects] colored by the modifications [*vṛtti*] of the intellect. //20//
Viśvanātha:
He shows its connection with Māyā.
"Kārya" means the body.
The causes are the sense organs, which are the instruments for achieving pleasure and pain;

the agents are the deities presiding over those organs. The meaning is that, through superimposition upon them, [Prakṛti] becomes transformed into the form of effects and so forth due to its association with the Puruṣa, and by means of its own function called "ignorance" (avidyā), she provides that superimposition.
The individual soul (*puruṣa-jīva*) alone is the cause for being the experiencer of the pleasures and pains produced by that [nature].

This is the sense: although agency, causality, and even the states of being an agent and an experiencer are indeed attributes of *prakṛti*, nevertheless, in respect to these states such as being an effect, the insentient aspect is predominant; however, in the experience consisting of the perception of pleasure and pain, the conscious aspect is predominant.
According to the principle that designations are made according to predominance, in the case of being an effect and so forth, *prakṛti* is the cause;
in the case of being an enjoyer, *puruṣa* is said to be the cause. //20//

Baladeva: Now, regarding those two which are conjoined, he states the distinction in their functions with the words "kārya... (the effect). The body is the "effect" because it is the means for knowledge and action; the senses are the "causes. In their agency—that is, in their modification into their respective forms—Prakṛti is the cause.
This is because of the subsequent statement, "For the Puruṣa, being situated in Prakṛti," which shows that through its own conjunction, the Puruṣa presides over Prakṛti, making it conscious.

However, presided over by that [Puruṣa], Prakṛti transforms itself according to the qualities of his karma and thus becomes the creator of various bodies and so forth. Thus, while the Puruṣa is the cause for the experience of pleasure and other sensations provided by Prakṛti, he alone is the agent in their enjoyment; this is the meaning.
The Puruṣa’s function consists in being the presiding authority over Prakṛti and the experiencer of pleasure and the like.
Furthermore, since that agency regarding the body and so forth belongs to *prakṛti* as its presiding controller, the agency of the *puruṣa* alone is primary.
Thus the author of the Sūtras says, "He is the agent, because the scriptures have purpose," and so forth.
However, the presiding control of the Supreme Lord Hari is unavoidable in all cases.
Thus it has been said, and it will also be stated [later]. //20//
For the person, situated in material nature, experiences the qualities born of nature; attachment to these qualities is the cause of his births in good and evil wombs. 13.21
Śrīdhara: Nevertheless, how can there be the state of being an enjoyer for that which is changeless and devoid of birth?
To this he says: "The Puruṣa," because (hi) [of the following reason].
The *puruṣa* abiding in *prakṛti* exists in a state of identity with the body, which is its effect;
therefore, it experiences the pleasure, pain, and so forth produced by that [body].

Furthermore, for this *puruṣa*, in whatever births occur within existing wombs such as those of gods and the like, or non-existing wombs such as those of animals and the like, there is "attachment to the *guṇas*"—that is, attachment to the senses which perform auspicious and inauspicious actions by means of the *guṇas*.
The meaning is "the cause. //21//
Madhusūdana:
Since the Puruṣa has attained identity [with Prakṛti], it is while remaining in Prakṛti that the Puruṣa experiences—that is, perceives—the qualities born of Prakṛti.

Therefore, regarding births in good or evil wombs which are the causes for perceiving the qualities born of Prakṛti, those who are born in good wombs—such as gods and others—experience the desired fruit characterized by Sattva.
The "unworthy wombs" are those of animals and so forth, for in them an undesirable fruit characterized by *tamas* is experienced.

Therefore, the cause of that [bondage] for this person is attachment to the *guṇas*—namely, the very conceit of identity with *prakṛti*, which consists of the *guṇas* of *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas*.
The meaning is that for him who is inherently unattached, there is no transmigratory existence (*saṃsāra*) of its own accord.

Alternatively, "attachment to the qualities" (*guṇa-saṅga*) means attachment to, or desire for, the qualities—sound and so forth—which consist of pleasure, pain, and delusion; this very thing is the cause of his births in good and evil wombs. For the Śruti says: "As is one's desire, so is one's resolve; as is one's resolve, so is the action one performs; and according to the action one performs, so is that which one attains" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.4.5).
Even in this view, one should understand that there is an identification with *prakṛti* by virtue of being its fundamental cause. //21//
Viśvanātha:

However, due to the superimposition (adhyāsa) caused by beginningless ignorance (anādy-avidyā), one considers even the attributes belonging to that [Self], such as agency and enjoyership, to be one's own.
It is precisely from this that its transmigratory existence (saṃsāra) arises; thus he says "the person" (puruṣa).
Abiding in *prakṛti*— that is, existing through identification with the body which is the effect of *prakṛti*—

one experiences the qualities born of *prakṛti*, such as grief, delusion, pleasure, and pain, which are actually attributes of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*), by falsely imagining them to be one's own.
The cause of this is attachment to the *guṇas*.
Although this Self is unattached, its attachment to bodies composed of the *guṇas* is imagined through ignorance (*avidyā*).

In response to the inquiry "where does it experience?", he says: in those births produced by auspicious and inauspicious karma within the wombs of gods and so forth when they exist, and within the wombs of animals and so forth when they do not exist. //21//

Baladeva: This clarifies that the agency for the superintendence of *prakṛti* and for the experience of sound and other objects belongs to the *puruṣa* alone, and it also shows the cause of the *puruṣa*'s association with *prakṛti*.

Although the *puruṣa* consists solely of the essence of consciousness and bliss, the *puruṣa*, abiding in *prakṛti* due to the impressions (*vāsanā*) of beginningless karma, presides over her and, through the body and senses produced by her, being distinguished by the vital breath (*prāṇa*), experiences—that is, perceives—the qualities such as pleasure and so forth produced by her. As to where this occurs, he says: "always" (*sad*).

Regarding those births and so forth that occur within various wombs—whether among gods, humans, and the like, or among animals, birds, and the like, which are fashioned as virtuous or non-virtuous—it is the Puruṣa alone who possesses agency therein.
He states the cause for that association with them by saying "the cause" (kāraṇam).
[The cause is] the quality of attachment (guṇa), which is non-attachment to the desire for objects composed of the beginningless qualities (guṇas).
The meaning is this: the individual soul (*jīva*) is beginningless and is colored by latent impressions (*vāsanā*) in the form of karma and the like.

Because it is an enjoyer, it desires objects of enjoyment; thus, as long as there is association with the Real (*sat*), it will resort to *prakṛti*, which is present through the desires and other factors directed toward those objects, until those various latent impressions are exhausted.
Upon their exhaustion, however, it enjoys the bliss of the abode of the Supreme Self, according to such scriptural passages as, "He attains all desires together with the wise Brahman."

As for the statements beginning with "from primordial matter" (*prakṛteḥ*), "the effect and the cause" (*kārya-kāraṇa*), "by primordial matter alone" (*prakṛtyaiva ca*), and "nothing other than the qualities" (*nānyaṃ guṇebhyaḥ*), those Sāṅkhyas who grasp only the superficial meaning claim that these are merely the impulsive assertions of primordial matter itself; for they believe that agency is possible for that which is insentient, like a clod of earth or a piece of wood.
However, agency indeed consists in being possessed of the material cause, immediate perception, desire to act, and volition.
And that [agency] belongs to the conscious being alone; thus the Śruti declares: "Consciousness (vijñāna) extends the sacrifice and also extends ritual acts.
For this is the seer, the toucher, the hearer, the taster, the smeller, the thinker, the knower, the doer—the Puruṣa whose nature is consciousness," and so forth.
As for the claim that her agency (*kartṛtva*) belongs to her because of the superimposition of consciousness (*caitanyādhyāsa*) due to the proximity (*sannidhāna*) of the person—that is not so;
for it is more easily stated that the agency of that [body] which is subordinate to the consciousness proximate to it belongs to that very [consciousness] which is proximate.
Indeed, it is observed that the burning power of heated iron is caused by fire alone, and not caused by the iron.

Nor is it the case that the insentient [Prakṛti] achieves its true nature through such [injunctions], just as water does not move or a tree bears fruit [merely by being told to do so]. This is because the establishment of its reality is untenable unless it is accepted as being presided over by an internal ruler (*antaryāmin*), which would contradict the scriptural injunctions that enjoin [action]. For the Smṛti does not enjoin sacrifices such as the Jyotiṣṭoma—which have heaven and the like as their fruits—nor meditation, with respect to the insentient Prakṛti; rather, it enjoins them with respect to the conscious enjoyer alone.
Agency belongs to the *puruṣa* alone;

as for what was said—that it [agency] belongs to *prakṛti*—that is due solely to the predominance of its functions (*vṛtti*). Just as there is the designation "the hand carries" when one carries with the hand, so too, when the *puruṣa* acts by means of *prakṛti*, the expression "prakṛti acts" may occur; thus say some.

Only the *puruṣa* who is joined with the material body and so forth possesses agency in actions such as sacrifice and battle, but not one who is separated from them and pure; therefore, others maintain that "that [agency] belongs to *prakṛti*. (BhG 13.22)
The supreme Person within this body is called the witness, the consenter, the sustainer, the enjoyer, the Great Lord, and also the Supreme Self. 22.
Śrīdhara: Thus, by this method, the transmigratory existence of the Puruṣa arises solely from the non-discrimination of Prakṛti, and not from its own essential nature.
With this intention, he states its true nature as "the witness" (upadraṣṭṛ).
Even while abiding in this body, which is the effect of primordial nature (prakṛti), the Person (puruṣa) remains supreme and distinct;
the meaning is that he is not joined with its qualities. The reasons for this are: because he is the "observer" (upadraṣṭā), meaning he stands nearby as a witness, being entirely separate.
Likewise, the one who permits is merely the one who consents, being a benefactor by his mere presence;
for so says scripture: "The witness, the conscious one, alone and devoid of qualities" (GTU 2.96, *Puruṣa-bodhinī*), and so forth.
Likewise, He is declared by the Śruti to be the Lord through His sovereignty and form, the Ordainer,
the Enjoyer, and the Protector;
and as the Great One and the Sovereign, He is called the Master even of Brahmā and the others, or the Supreme Self and the Inner Ruler.
And thus says the Śruti: "He is the Lord of all, He is the Sovereign of beings, the Protector of the world," and so forth. //22//
Madhusūdana:
Thus it has been stated that the transmigratory existence (*saṃsāra*) of the *puruṣa* arises from its false identity with *prakṛti*, and not by way of its own essential nature (*svarūpa*).
What, then, is that essential nature of his in which transmigratory existence is impossible?
To this inquiry, [the Lord], directly indicating its essential nature, says: "The witness" (*upadraṣṭṛ*).

Although the Puruṣa exists in this body—which is a transformation of *prakṛti*—in the form of the individual soul (*jīva*), he is transcendent (*para*), unattached to the qualities of *prakṛti*, and in the ultimate sense, not subject to transmigratory existence by his own nature; such is the meaning. Because he is a witness, just as when the officiating priests and the sacrificer are occupied with the sacrificial rites, another person standing near them, though himself unoccupied, [observes] the merits and defects of the activities of the priests and the sacrificer due to his proficiency in the science of sacrifice.

In the same way, the Puruṣa, himself not engaged in the activities of the organs and the body, is distinct from them; standing near those organs and the body which are possessed of activity, he is the witness, but not the agent.
For the Śruti says: "Whatever he sees there, he is not followed by it; for this Puruṣa is unattached" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.3.15).
Alternatively, among the seers consisting of the body, the eyes, the mind, the intellect, and the self, the innermost seer—the Self, which is the Person—is the "witness" (*upadraṣṭṛ*).
This is because the prefix *upa-* signifies proximity, and that proximity culminates precisely in the inward-turned Self, being of the nature of non-intervention.

Furthermore, He is the "consenter" (*anumantṛ*); although not Himself engaged in the activities of the organs and instruments, He is like one who has engaged in them, being a consenter by His mere presence due to His conformity with those activities.
Alternatively, the Puruṣa, being the witness (*sākṣin*) to the body, senses, and so forth as they engage in their respective functions, never obstructs them; thus, he is the "consenter" (*anumantṛ*).

This is according to the Śruti: "The witness, the cognizer" (GTU 2.96, *Puruṣa-bodhinī*). He is the "supporter" (*bhartṛ*): by his own existence and by his manifestation, he is the sustainer and nourisher of the body, senses, mind, and intellect when they are combined and characterized by the reflection of consciousness (*caitanyābhāsa*).
The enjoyer, by illuminating through its own essential consciousness the mental modifications consisting of pleasure, pain, and delusion, remains indeed changeless as the perceiver.
It is the Great Lord (Maheśvara) because it is the Self of all and, being independent, is both great and a lord.

It is the Supreme Self (Paramātman), the supreme and most excellent Self, distinguished by the previously mentioned attributes such as being the witness, with respect to everything from the body up to the intellect which are falsely imagined as the Self through ignorance.
By this word "it" (iti), He has been spoken of and described in the Śruti;
by the word "ca" (and), that same Supreme Person is also indicated by such terms as "the Witness" (upadraṣṭṛ) and so forth.
As will be stated later: "But the Supreme Person is another, declared to be the Supreme Self" (Gītā 15.17). //22//
Viśvanātha:
Having spoken of the individual soul (jīvātman), he speaks of the Supreme Self (paramātman) with the words "the witness" (upadraṣṭṛ).

Although the Supreme Self has indeed already been described both generally and specifically by such passages as "without beginning, beyond the Great" (anādimat-param brahma) and "established in the heart of all" (hṛdi sarvasya viṣṭhitam), [He is now mentioned again].
This statement should be understood as being made for the purpose of clearly indicating that even in association with the individual soul (jīvātman), He remains distinct and dwells within the body.
Furthermore, it is said that the Supreme Person, who is the Great Lord (maheśvara) and other than this [individual], is the Supreme Self (paramātman);
the meaning is that He is also designated by the name "Supreme Self."

In this context, the word "supreme" (*parama*) serves to illuminate that, according to the doctrine of a single self (*ekātmavāda*), it is one's own part (*svāṃśa*). The witness (*sākṣin*) is the observer who stands distinct and in proximity (*upa*) to the individual soul (*jīva*); he is the approver (*anumantṛ*), the agent of consent, and the benefactor by mere presence.
As it is said: "The witness, the cognizer, alone and devoid of qualities" (GTU 2.96).
This is according to the Śruti: "The Puruṣa-bodhinī.
Likewise, [the Lord is] the sustainer (bhartā), the supporter (dhāraka), the enjoyer (bhoktā), and the protector (pālaka).

Baladeva, having described the individual soul (jīva) as residing in the body as the enjoyer of pleasure and so forth, speaks of the Lord (Īśvara) residing therein as the controller by saying "the overseer" (upadraṣṭṛ).

In this body, there exists another Person, distinct from the individual soul (jīva), who is called Maheśvara or the Supreme Self (paramātman). He is the "observer" (upadraṣṭṛ), standing apart in proximity as the witness;
He is the "consenter" (anumantṛ), the giver of permission, meaning that without His consent, the individual soul is not capable of performing even the slightest action.
The Lord (īśa) is the sustainer (bhartṛ), meaning the supporter;
He is the enjoyer (bhoktṛ), meaning the protector.
Although He has already been described by such terms as "having hands everywhere," this repetition is intended to state His coexistence with the individual soul (jīva). //22//
He who thus knows the Puruṣa and Prakṛti along with its qualities (guṇas), in whatever way he may live, is not born again. 13.23.
Śrīdhara: Thus he praises the one who possesses the knowledge of the discrimination between *prakṛti* and *puruṣa* with the words "He who thus...

He who knows the *puruṣa* in the form of the witness (*upadraṣṭṛ*) and so forth, and who knows *prakṛti* along with its qualities (*guṇas*) together with their transformations such as pleasure and pain—that *puruṣa*, even while existing here having completely transgressed the injunctions, is not born again.
The meaning is that he is indeed liberated. //23//
Madhusūdana:
Thus, the verse "And who He is, and what His power is" (Gītā 13.4) has been explained. Now, he concludes the statement "Knowing which, one attains immortality" with the words "He who thus...
He who knows in the manner described—that is, who realizes directly that "I am this Puruṣa"—and [knows] Prakṛti, which is ignorance; |||

Through the knowledge of the Self, he knows that [the world]—together with its qualities and its own transformations—is false and has been sublated; thus, when his ignorance and its effects have ceased, even though he continues to exist by the force of *prārabdha*-karma, transgressing the injunctions like Indra, he is not born again; once this body of the knower has fallen, he does not take up another body.

Since it has been stated in many ways that when ignorance (*avidyā*) is destroyed by knowledge (*vidyā*), its effects cannot possibly arise, it follows from the principle: "Upon the attainment of that [Self], there is the non-clinging of future karma and the destruction of past karma, because of the scriptural designation thereof" (VS 4.1.13). By the force of the word "also" (*api*), the intention is: what need is there to say that one who lives according to the injunctions, remaining established in his own nature, is not born again? //23//

Viśvanātha: He states the fruit of this knowledge with the words "He who... [referring to the verse beginning with *yaḥ*]. "The Person" (*puruṣam*) is the Supreme Self (*paramātman*); "Prakṛti" is the power of illusion (*māyā-śakti*).
And by the word "ca" (and), [the text includes] the power of the individual soul (*jīva-śakti*).
Even though existing in every way, even if overcome by dissolution, distraction, and so forth. //23//
Baladeva: He states the fruit of this knowledge with the word "yaḥ" (who).

Thus, by the method described by Me, he who knows the Puruṣa, Prakṛti, and the Jīva as mutually distinct—meaning that even while existing in constant contact with worldly affairs—he is not born again; the sense is that he is liberated at the end of the body. //23//
13.24 Some perceive the Self within the self by means of meditation through the self;
others by the yoga of Sāṃkhya, and still others by the yoga of action.
Śrīdhara: With the two verses beginning with "By meditation" (dhyānena), he states the various means for attaining such knowledge of the isolated Self.
By "meditation" (dhyānena) is meant the repetition of cognitions having the form of the Self.
In this way, some perceive the Self within the very body by means of the Self—that is, by the mind.

Others, however, perceive [the Self] through Sāṅkhya, by means of the yoga consisting of the contemplation of the distinction between Prakṛti and Puruṣa; and others through the eightfold Yoga, and still others through Karma-yoga—
the phrase "they perceive" is to be supplied in each case.

And although there is a sequential compounding of these [practices], such as the meditative absorptions (dhyāna) and so forth, according to what is appropriate, the statement of alternatives is made with the intention of referring to the specific distinctions in their respective culminations. //24//
Madhusūdana:
Here, these alternative means for the realization of the Self are stated, beginning with "by meditation.
For in this world, there are four types of people.
Some are superior, some are middling, some are dull, and some are even more dull.
Among them, he describes the means for those who are superior to realize the Self:

through meditation (*dhyāna*), which consists of a continuous flow of homogeneous mental impressions (*sajātīya-pratyaya*) uninterrupted by heterogeneous impressions, and which is the fruit of hearing (*śravaṇa*) and reflection (*manana*), namely, the contemplation of the Self.

By means of the inner organ purified through meditation, certain superior yogins perceive—that is, directly realize—the Self within the intellect, which is the inwardly conscious Self, as denoted by the term "nididhyāsana.
Regarding the means for those of middling capacity to know the Self, he says: others, who are of middling capacity, [attain it] through the yoga of Sāṃkhya, which precedes nididhyāsana.

Through the process of hearing and reflection preceded by the discrimination between the eternal and the non-eternal, they perceive the Self as "I am the Self"—that is, they see the Self through contemplation born from the inquiry into Vedāntic statements, [realizing]: "All these transformations of the three qualities are non-self and entirely illusory; whereas the witness of that [phenomenon] is the eternal, all-pervading, changeless, true Self, devoid of any connection with all that is insentient. This is how the text proceeds.
The meaning is "by means of meditation as the door of arising.

He states the means of knowledge for those of dull intellect: "And others, the dull-witted, perceive the Self by the Self through the yoga of action"—that is, by the collection of actions prescribed in the Vedas, appropriate to their respective caste and stage of life, performed with the intellect of dedication to the Lord, free from desire for fruits. The phrase "perceive the Self by the Self" continues [from the previous verse].
The meaning is: by means of the purification of the mind (sattva), through the arising of hearing, reflection, and meditation. //24//
Viśvanātha:
Here, he states the alternative means of accomplishment in two verses beginning with "dhyāna.
Some devotees [attain it] through meditation alone—that is, through the contemplation of the Blessed One.

Based on the subsequent statement, "By devotion he comes to know Me" (Gītā 18.55), the meaning is that one knows Me within oneself by means of the self, by oneself alone, and not through any other auxiliary means.
Others—namely the knowers of reality (jñānins)—know through *sāṅkhya*, which is the discrimination between the self and the non-self;
others—the practitioners of yoga (yogins)—know through *yoga*, namely the eightfold yoga and through selfless action (*niṣkāma-karman*).

In this regard, the Sāṅkhya, the eightfold yoga (aṣṭāṅga-yoga), and the yoga of desireless action (niṣkāma-karma-yoga) are causes for the vision of the Supreme Self only through their mutual interaction, and not direct causes, because they are characterized by the quality of goodness (sattva), whereas the Supreme Self transcends the qualities (guṇātīta). Furthermore, following the Lord’s statement, "And one should surrender knowledge unto Me" (BhP 11.19.1), after the renunciation of knowledge and the other [means],...
Because of the statement, "In this way, I am to be grasped by exclusive devotion alone" (BhP 11.14.11), they perceive [the Lord] through that very devotion, setting aside knowledge. //24//
Baladeva: With two verses beginning with "By meditation," he describes the various means for attaining Maheśvara.

Certain ones of purified mind perceive Me, the Self, who am Maheśvara, abiding within the self—that is, the mind—through meditation, wherein knowledge is subordinate; they realize Me directly by themselves alone, and not through any other external aid.

Others perceive through knowledge in which meditation is subordinate, according to the Sāṅkhya system; others perceive through the eightfold yoga in which knowledge is subordinate; while still others perceive through the yoga of action—action performed without desire, in which both meditation and knowledge are included. //24//
But others, not knowing thus, worship having heard it from others;
they too, being devoted to what they have heard, certainly cross over death. (13.25)
Śrīdhara: He states "others" as the means of liberation for those of very dull faculties.

Others, however, being unable to directly realize the Self characterized by such qualities as being the witness (upadraṣṭṛtva) through the paths of Sāṅkhya, Yoga, and so forth, meditate upon it—that is, they contemplate it—having heard of it from other teachers by way of instruction.
And they too, being devoted to hearing the instruction with faith, gradually transcend death and saṃsāra. //25//
Madhusūdana:
With the word "others," he states the means of knowledge for those who are even more dull-witted.
"Others," however, refers to those who are very dull-witted.
The word *tu* (but) is intended to highlight the distinction between these [seekers] and the three types of qualified aspirants mentioned in the preceding verse.

Among these means, even by one or another, those who do not thus know the Self as described, having heard from other compassionate teachers, "Meditate upon this very thing," being full of faith, they worship— that is,
they reflect upon it.

Even they certainly transcend death and saṃsāra, being devoted to the sacred teachings (śruti); for although they are themselves incapable of inquiry, they are solely intent on hearing the instructions of the guru through their faith.
By the word "even" (api) in the phrase "even they," the intention is: what need is there to mention that those who are themselves capable of inquiry transcend death? //25//
Viśvanātha:
Others are listeners of the story here and there. //25//

Baladeva: But others, not knowing such means as these, being devoted to the Śruti and intent upon hearing the various accounts [of the Lord] and so forth, hear those means from other speakers and worship that Great Lord. They, as well as their associates, gradually attain and practice those means and certainly transcend death; thus, the extraordinary greatness of hearing the accounts of Him is demonstrated. //25//
Whatever being is born, whether stationary or moving, know that, O bull among the Bharatas, it arises from the union of the field and the Knower of the field. 13.26

Śrīdhara: Now, since *karma-yoga* has been elaborated upon in the third, fourth, and fifth chapters, and *dhyāna-yoga* has been elaborated upon in the sixth and eighth, and since *dhyāna* and the other forms of yoga have as their object the self (*ātman*) as distinguished [from the constituents] in Sāṅkhya, [the Lord], while elaborating upon Sāṅkhya itself, says "as long as" and so forth, up to the end of the chapter.

Know that whatever mere object or being arises, all of it comes about through the conjunction of the field and the knower of the field, due to the superimposition of identity produced by non-discrimination. //26//
Madhusūdana:

In order to establish the point that liberation through knowledge is possible because transmigratory existence (*saṃsāra*) is rooted in ignorance (*avidyā*), an exposition of transmigratory existence and the knowledge that removes it is undertaken until the end of this chapter.

Regarding this, he explains what was previously stated in the verse, "The cause of this is attachment to the qualities (*guṇa-saṅga*), which leads to births in good and evil wombs" (Gītā 13.21), by means of the word "yāvat" (until).

Whatever being or object arises—whether stationary or moving—all that is the field (*kṣetra*), consisting of ignorance and its effects, insentient, indefinable, and of a nature that is neither existent nor non-existent; it is the entire range of the visible. Distinct from that is the Knower of the Field (*kṣetrajña*): self-luminous, ultimate reality, pure consciousness, unattached, indifferent, devoid of attributes, and non-dual.

The Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña) and these two [Prakṛti and the intellect]— their conjunction, caused by the failure to distinguish between them due to the power of Māyā, is a false superimposition (adhyāsa) consisting of the identification of one with the other, which consists in the coupling of the real and the unreal.
Know, O bull among the Bharatas, that from this alone all that collection of effects is produced.

Therefore, the intention is that transmigratory existence, which is rooted in ignorance of one's true nature, deserves to perish through the knowledge of that true nature, just like a dream and so forth. //26//
Viśvanātha:
He elaborates upon the very point already stated until the end of the chapter.
"As far as" (*yāvat*) means whatever measure there may be, whether inferior or superior.
Sattva refers to any living being whatsoever. //26//

Baladeva: Now, for the purpose of investigating the union of primordial nature (*prakṛti*) and the individual soul (*jīva*), which have been joined from time immemorial, he first describes their creation through that conjunction with the words "as far as" (*yāvat*).

Whatever being—whether stationary or moving, whatever living creature—is born, in whatever measure, whether superior or inferior, know that it arises from the conjunction of the field (*kṣetra*) and the knower of the field (*kṣetrajña*).
The meaning is: understand that it comes into existence through the relationship of the knower of the field with the field, which is primordial nature.
The Lord, governing both primordial nature (prakṛti) and the individual soul (jīva), sets them in motion; these two, moreover, bind one another.
Thus, the meaning is that the creation of living beings occurs through the medium of the production of bodies. //26//
He truly sees who perceives the Supreme Lord abiding equally in all beings, the imperishable within the perishing. 13.27

Śrīdhara: Having stated that the origin of saṃsāra is caused by a lack of discrimination, he declares the right vision (samyag-darśana) concerning the distinct Self for the sake of its cessation with the word "sama" (equal).
He who perceives the Supreme Self as remaining equal—without distinction—in all beings consisting of the moving and the stationary, by virtue of Its nature as Pure Being;
and for that very reason, he who perceives It as not perishing even when they perish—he alone [is a seer].
He sees correctly. //27//
Madhusūdana:

Having thus described *saṃsāra* as consisting of ignorance (*avidyā*), he now explains the verse beginning with "He who knows the Person thus" (*ya evaṃ vetti puruṣam*)—which was previously mentioned—in order to explain the knowledge that brings about its cessation, starting with the word "equal" (*samam*).

[The Lord dwells] in all beings—that is, in all living creatures characterized by the nature of coming into existence, consisting of both the stationary and the moving, and subject to various transformations such as birth and so forth.

Furthermore, because they fall into a state of being either subordinate or primary, things are therefore unstable; for all phenomena undergo transformation at every moment and are not capable of remaining even for an instant without changing.
Consequently, while they are thus subject to a mutual relationship of the sublated and the sublator, and are seen to perish, their very nature is one of disappearance.

When all duality— consisting mostly of illusions, cities of the Gandharvas, and the like— is seen to be as good as vanished, there remains the Supreme Lord, who is uniform and of one nature everywhere, who abides as one within every body, who is unchanging due to being devoid of transformations such as birth and so forth, who bestows existence and manifestation upon the entire aggregate of insentient things, who is free from the relationship of sublated and sublator, who is untainted by any defects, and who is imperishable.
This too is uncontradicted.

Thus, he who perceives the Self— which is in every respect distinct from the insentient phenomenal world— through the eye of the scriptures by means of discrimination, he alone truly sees the Self, just as one dispelling a dream-delusion through waking consciousness.
But the ignorant person, like one seeing a dream, perceives erroneously through delusion and thus does not see at all;
for since delusion consists in non-perception,
one who sees a rope as a snake is not said to "see" it.

Because the perception of a snake consists in the non-perception of the rope, so too, from the vision of the pure Self uncolored by [adjuncts], there is the cessation of that ignorance which consists in the perception of those [adjuncts]; from that follows the cessation of saṃsāra, which is the effect of that [ignorance]. This is the intended meaning. Here, the term "Self" (*ātmānam*) acquires its specific referent through the force of the qualification.
Alternatively, "the Supreme Lord" (*parameśvara*) itself is the qualifying term (*viśeṣya-pada*).

The distinction residing in the insentient—characterized by inequality, instability, and the nature of the sublated and the sublator—is implicitly obtained through the force of the qualifiers of the Self, namely equality, stability, and the state of being the Supreme Lord; thus, the distinction is that one [aspect] is explicitly stated while the other is implied. //27//
Viśvanātha:
He says "equal" (samam) to indicate that one should know the Supreme Self in this way:
he who perceives [the Self] even as bodies perish.
The meaning is that he alone is the one possessed of knowledge. //27//

Baladeva: Now, [the Lord] says "equal" (samam) to show that one should perceive the Lord—who, though residing within primordial nature (prakṛti) and the individual souls (jīvas) conjoined with it—as distinct from them.

However, the one who does not know reality, being attached, perceives the Supreme Lord—who abides equally and with a single essence in all beings, whether stationary or moving, that is, in all embodied souls—as perishing along with the destruction of their respective bodies.

While those [individual souls] are undergoing destruction, he who perceives that which does not perish—the witness of them—truly sees; he alone becomes a seer of reality as it is (*tad-yāthātmya-darśī*).

Thus, the Supreme Lord is distinct from the individual souls (*jīvas*), which possess the nature of diversity and destruction and are conjoined with *prakṛti*, because He is characterized by uniformity and indestructibility. //27//
For seeing the Lord established equally everywhere, one does not destroy the self by means of the self; therefore, one goes to the supreme goal. 28.
Śrīdhara asks: "Why? To this he says: "Equally" (samam).
Seeing the Supreme Self as equally—meaning correctly—abiding with its own nature unimpaired in all things, that is, in all mere beings (bhūtamātra).
For indeed, by itself, it does not harm itself;
having veiled its own nature— which consists of existence, consciousness, and bliss— through ignorance, it does not destroy it,
and thereby it attains the supreme goal, which is liberation.
But he who does not see thus—being one who perceives the self in the body—he destroys the self along with the body.
And so says the Śruti:
"Sunless indeed are those worlds, shrouded in blind darkness."
"Those people who are slayers of the Self go to them after death" (Īśa Upaniṣad 3).
Thus [ends the citation]. Madhusūdana [comments]: He praises this very vision of the Self with its fruit in order to generate a desire for it, saying "equal."
Because it is empty of the modifications of existence beginning with birth and ending with destruction, there is the attainment of abiding correctly in its state of imperishability.
The rest has been explained previously.
Thus, seeing the Self endowed with the aforementioned qualifications, and realizing through the vision of the scriptures that "I am this," one does not destroy the self by means of the self.

For every ignorant person, by means of ignorance— which is capable of producing the cognition that "it does not exist" and "it does not appear," even though the reality exists— himself obscures the Self, which is in truth one, the non-agent, the non-enjoyer, and the nature of supreme bliss; thus, making it as if non-existent, he indeed destroys it.
Thus, having destroyed the former self—the aggregate of body and senses which has been grasped as the self through ignorance—one takes up a new one under the influence of karma;
therefore, in either case, every ignorant person is indeed a slayer of the self.
It is with reference to such a person that this traditional teaching (smṛti) in the form of Śakuntalā’s words was spoken:
"What sin has not been committed by that thief who robs himself, who represents himself as one thing when he is otherwise? And so says the Śruti:
"Sunless indeed are those worlds, enveloped in blind darkness;
to them go after death those people who are slayers of the Self. (Īśa Upaniṣad 3).
Here, "sunless" means they are the domain of the Asura, to be experienced through the demonic state (*āsuryā saṃpat*).
"Self-destroyers" means those who have the conceit of "self" in what is not-self.
Therefore, he who knows the Self sublates the conceit of self in the non-self by means of the vision of the pure Self.
Thus, through the recovery of his true nature, he destroys himself by himself, and thereby attains the supreme goal.
Therefore, because there is no self-destruction, the meaning is that one attains liberation characterized by the cessation of ignorance and its effects.
Viśvanātha:
By means of the self—that is, the mind—which does not travel on a wrong path, one does not destroy, nor cause to fall downward, the self, which is the individual soul (jīva). //28//

Baladeva: Then, with the intention that one perceives the Lord as distinct from those aforementioned objects and, by the power of that perception, attains self-discrimination from the transformations of *prakṛti*, he says:
"Seeing [the Lord] as equal, indeed..."—meaning, seeing Him equally in all beings, existing exactly as He is, with His essential nature and qualities remaining perfectly unaltered.

Seeing the Lord as his own Self by means of the mind—which perceives the distinction between primordial nature (*prakṛti*) and its transformations, yet remains greedy for the flavors of sense objects—he does not harm nor cause himself to fall downward;

rather, through that same mind which has become dispassionate toward those flavors, he attains the supreme, most excellent goal: the discernment of his own distinctness from those transformations. //28//
He who sees that all actions are being performed in every way by nature alone, and likewise sees the Self as the non-doer— he truly sees. (13.29)

Śrīdhara: Now, raising the objection—"Since inequality is observed in the state of being the agent of auspicious and inauspicious karma, how can the Self be equanimous?"—he says: "By nature alone," meaning by nature alone as transformed into the form of the body and senses;
"in every way," meaning in all modes.
He who perceives actions as being performed, and likewise perceives himself as a non-agent— since the self’s agency arises only through the identification with the body and not by its own nature—
he alone sees correctly.
The meaning is that there is no other [agent].

Madhusūdana [raises an objection]: "But surely, the performers of auspicious and inauspicious karma are distinct for each body, and the selves are diverse, by virtue of being the experiencers of those various corresponding fruits."
