It has been stated: "How is it that one who sees the single Self as equal, abiding in all beings, does not destroy the self by means of the self?
To this he says: "By nature alone...
Actions—those initiated by speech, mind, and body—in every way and by all means, are performed by nature alone, which has transformed itself into the form of the aggregate of the body and the senses.

He who is discerning perceives that all modifications are being produced solely by the Lord’s Māyā— which consists of the three *guṇas* and is the cause of all transformations— and not by the *puruṣa*, who is devoid of all modifications;

likewise, even while actions are being performed by the *kṣetra*, he who perceives the Self as the Knower of the Field (*kṣetrajña*)— the non-agent, free from all adjuncts, unattached, one, and equal everywhere.
The word "tathā" (thus) serves to draw in the action "he sees";
as before, it means "he sees, he is the seer of ultimate reality.
[This applies] to the field (kṣetra), which undergoes modification, by virtue of its being the agent of various respective actions in each body.

Even if there were division or inequality, there is no evidence whatsoever for the division of the Self—which is devoid of distinctions and inactive—just as there is none for space; this has been established previously. //29//
Viśvanātha:

By its very nature, [Māyā], having transformed itself in every way into the form of the body, senses, and so forth, causes the Self—the individual soul (jīva)—to perceive itself as the agent through the very conceit of being the body;
however, this is not due to its own inherent nature.
The meaning is: "he who perceives in this manner. //29//

Baladeva: In response to the inquiry as to how one attains discrimination between the self and primordial nature (*prakṛti*), he states the method therein with two verses beginning with "by primordial nature itself" (*prakṛtyaiva*).
He who perceives all actions as being performed by primordial nature alone—impelled by the Lord and presided over by Me—and likewise perceives the self as the non-doer of those actions;
He alone sees; he becomes a seer of his own true nature.
This is the meaning: "I am certainly not of the nature of consciousness and bliss performing actions such as battle and sacrifice, which consist of suffering;

rather, it is through my body and other instruments that [action is performed] by me—who am presided over by beginningless impressions of enjoyment and who am devoid of discrimination—for the sake of accomplishing my own enjoyment."

It performs those [actions] because it has them as its cause; thus, since that very [nature] is the agent of that, the pure *jīva*—distinct from and not the agent of that—is separate from the primordial nature (*prakṛti*) which is the agent.
Furthermore, the agency of even the pure [self] is made explicit by the phrase "he perceives."
When one perceives the diversity of beings as abiding in the One, and likewise their expansion from that very source, then one attains Brahman. (13.30)

Śrīdhara: Now, however, because even the elements (*bhūta*) are non-different from *prakṛti* insofar as they consist of nothing more than that, one who does not perceive any distinction of the self (*ātman*) caused by the distinction between elements attains the state of Brahman; thus he says, "When...

When he perceives—that is, contemplates—the separate existence, the difference, the distinctness of all beings, both stationary and moving, as being situated in one place, namely in *prakṛti*, which at the time of dissolution exists as a single power of the Lord.
Therefore, at the time of creation, he perceives the expansion of the elements from that very Prakṛti;
then, seeing that the elements are non-different from Prakṛti alone, he attains the perfect Brahman—the meaning is that he becomes Brahman itself. //30//
Madhusūdana:

Thus, having first rejected the perception of a distinction between fields by not conceding it at the outset, he now rejects even the perception of a distinction between fields on the grounds that it is illusory (*māyika*), beginning with the words "When...
(*yadā*).

When— at whatever time— one perceives, through the instruction of the scriptures and the teacher, that the separate existence— the distinctness or mutual difference— of all beings, both stationary and moving, as well as of the entire class of insentient things, resides in the One, namely, in the Self whose nature is Being; and that this perceived difference does not exceed the substratum of that which is imagined, being non-different from the essential nature of the Self which is Being.
He reflects for himself: "The Self alone is all this" (ChāU 7.25.2).
Even so, by the power of *māyā*, he perceives the expansion from that single Self and the separate existence of beings as being like a dream or an illusion;
when he has thus attained Brahman, then, due to the absence of any perception of difference—whether of the same kind or of a different kind—he is indeed Brahman.
At that time, all misfortune becomes void,
when for the one who knows, all beings have become the Self alone. What delusion, what sorrow can there be for him who perceives this oneness?
This is according to the Śruti [Īśa Upaniṣad 7].
In the verse beginning with "prakṛtyaiva ca" (and by nature alone), the differentiation of the Self is refuted;

however, in the verse beginning with "yadā bhūta-pṛthag-bhāvam" (when [one perceives] the separate existence of beings), there is the further distinction that the differentiation of the non-Self is also refuted. //30//

Viśvanātha: When one perceives— that is, contemplates— at the time of dissolution (*pralaya*), that the separate existence of beings, both stationary and moving, their distinctness as they exist in their respective forms, is "situated in one," namely, situated in *prakṛti* alone.
Then, at the time of creation, he perceives the expansion of the elements from Prakṛti itself; at that moment, he attains Brahman—meaning he becomes Brahman. //30//
Baladeva: Regarding the phrase "when" (*yadā*):

when this individual soul (*jīva*) perceives, during the dissolution (*pralaya*), the distinctness of beings—such as gods, humans, and others—which consists of their respective forms like divinity, humanity, tallness, and shortness, as being unified and residing solely within *prakṛti*; then, at the time of creation, those states of divinity and so forth arise from *prakṛti* alone.
He perceives its expansion,
yet he does not perceive that state of separateness as residing within himself, nor does he perceive that expansion as belonging to the self;
he is one who perceives the self as distinct from its own inherent nature.

The meaning is that then one attains that Brahman; being distinct from it, one experiences for oneself one's own nature, which is characterized by the eight great qualities such as freedom from sin and so forth. //30//
Because it is beginningless and devoid of qualities, this supreme Self is immutable; O son of Kuntī, although dwelling within the body, it neither acts nor is it tainted. (13.31)

Śrīdhara: Even so, since the Supreme Lord, while in the state of worldly existence, is subject to inequality caused by actions and their fruits—such as pleasure and pain—arising from his connection with a body, how can there be "equal vision"? To this, he says: "Because of beginninglessness."
For that alone which has an origin perishes, that is, it undergoes destruction;
and for that entity which possesses qualities, there is perishing when its qualities perish.
But this Supreme Self is beginningless and devoid of qualities.
Therefore, the meaning is that he is imperishable and changeless.
Consequently, even while situated in the body, he does nothing at all, nor is he tainted by the fruits of actions. //31//
Madhusūdana:

Dispelling the doubt that even though the Self is inherently a non-agent (*akartṛ*), agency might arise due to the limiting condition (*upādhi*) of its connection with a body, he explains the statement "he who sees thus... he sees" by means of the verse beginning with "without beginning."

This immediate inner self (*pratyag-ātman*) is non-different from the Supreme Self (*paramātman*), the Supreme Lord (*parameśvara*); it is "imperishable" (*avyaya*), meaning it does not perish, that is to say, it is devoid of all modifications. In this context, "perishing" (*vyaya*) is twofold: either by the very nature of the substratum (*dharmin*) being subject to origination, or, even if the nature of the substratum is unoriginated, by the qualities (*dharmas*) themselves being subject to origination and so forth. Of these, he refutes the first [possibility] by stating, "because it is beginningless" (*anāditvāt*).
The "beginning" is the prior state of non-existence;
and that does not exist for the self, which is eternally existent.
Therefore, due to the absence of a cause, there is an absence of birth for it.
For birth is not possible for that which is beginningless;
and in its absence, the modifications of existence (bhāva-vikāra) that follow it cannot possibly occur.
Therefore, the meaning is that it does not perish by way of its own essential nature (svarūpa).
He refutes the second [position] with the words "because of being devoid of qualities" (*nirguṇatvāt*).
The meaning is "because of being devoid of attributes" (*nirdharmakatvāt*).

For no attribute whatsoever can approach or depart without affecting the substratum (*dharmin*), because of the identity (*tādātmya*) between attribute and substratum; however, since this [entity] is devoid of attributes, it does not pass away even by way of its attributes—this is the meaning.
For the Śruti declares: "Verily, this Self is indestructible, for it is of a nature that does not perish" (BAU 4.5.14).

Since this Self is devoid of the six modifications of being—namely, being born, existing, growing, transforming, declining, and perishing—it does not act, even while residing in the body through a superimposed connection, despite that body performing actions.
Just as the sun situated in water does not move even when that [water] moves due to its relation as a superimposition (*adhyāsika-sambandha*), so too [the Self is not affected].
For the meaning is that this [Self] is not tainted, not because of being a non-agent (*akartṛtva*),
but because desire, hatred, pleasure, pain, and so forth have been declared to be attributes of the field (*kṣetra*).
Furthermore, because actions are performed by their very nature, they are designated as the effects of *māyā*.
For this very reason, it was explained previously that for those who perceive the ultimate reality (*paramārtha*), there is a cessation of all qualification for ritual action (*karma*).
By this statement that the Self is devoid of attributes (*nirdharmaka*), even internal difference (*svagata-bheda*) is refuted.
By the verse "actions are by nature alone" (*Gītā* 13.29), difference among those of the same class (*sajātīya-bheda*) is precluded;
and by the verse "when [one perceives] the distinctness of beings" (*Gītā* 13.30), difference among those of different classes (*vijātīya-bheda*) is [precluded].

In the verse beginning "Because it is beginningless and devoid of qualities" (Gītā 13.31), it is established that internal differentiation does not exist; thus, the non-dual Brahman alone is the Self. //31//
Viśvanātha:
Now, it has been stated that "attachment to the qualities is the cause of this [self's] births in good and evil wombs.

In that regard, although they are equal insofar as both reside within the body, it is only the individual self (jīvātman) that is smeared by the qualities and transmigrates, and not the Supreme Self (paramātman).
To the question "Why?", he says: "Because of beginninglessness" (*anāditvāt*).
That which has no beginning—that is, no cause—is "beginningless.
Just as the word *anuttama* (unsurpassed), ending in the fifth case, denotes the supreme excellence, so too the word *anādi* (beginningless) denotes the ultimate cause.

Furthermore, because He is beginningless, the supreme cause, and devoid of qualities—meaning that from whom the qualities such as creation and so forth have departed—His state is His true nature (*tattva*). Therefore, this Supreme Self is distinct from the individual soul (*jīvātman*);
He is imperishable, eternally and in every way free from the decay of His own knowledge, bliss, and other attributes.
Although situated within the body, because He does not assume its characteristics, He does not act like the individual soul; He is not an agent.
He does not become an enjoyer, nor is he defiled; he is not smeared by the qualities of the body. //31//

Baladeva: [Objection: But is it not improper to say that one becomes fulfilled by perceiving the Supreme Lord and the self as distinct, given the scriptural teaching that the individual soul arises from these very elements and perishes along with them, and that after death there is no consciousness? To this, he says: "Because of beginninglessness" (*anāditvāt*).

This self, the living soul (*jīva*), although residing within the body, is by virtue of being beginningless, supreme, and immutable; because its primary nature is immutability, it is devoid of destruction; and because it is free from qualities (*nirguṇa*) and consists of pure knowledge and bliss, it does not perform actions such as battle or sacrifice.
Therefore, it is not tainted by the nature of the body and senses, which are characterized by birth and destruction.
But the meaning of the scriptural statement is to be understood in a figurative sense. //31//
Just as the all-pervading ether is not defiled because of its subtlety, so the Self, though situated everywhere within the body, is not defiled. 13.32
Śrīdhara: He states the reason for this, along with an illustration, beginning with "yathā" (just as).

Just as the all-pervading ether (*ākāśa*), though situated even within mud and the like, is not defiled by mud and so forth due to its subtlety and lack of attachment, so too the Self (*ātman*), although abiding everywhere—in a superior, middling, or inferior body—is not defiled. //32//
Madhusūdana:
[The Lord] says "just as" (yathā) to provide an illustration for the point that, although situated within the body, He is not tainted by its actions because He Himself is unattached.
The meaning of the illustration is that just as space, though all-pervading, is not defiled by mud and the like due to its subtlety and its inherent nature of non-attachment.
The rest is clear. //32//
Viśvanātha:

Now he states an illustration: just as space, though situated everywhere even within mud and the like, is not stained by mud and so forth due to its subtlety and lack of attachment, in the very same way, the Supreme Self is not joined with the qualities or defects pertaining to the body; this is the meaning. //32//
Baladeva: Now, as to why one situated in the body is not tainted by its qualities, he says "just as" (yathā).

Just as space, though it has gone into—that is, entered—everything such as mud and the like, is not tainted by their respective qualities due to its subtlety, so too the Self, the individual soul (jīva), though situated in every kind of high or low body, whether divine or human, is not tainted by their qualities precisely because of its subtlety. //32//
Just as the one sun illumines this entire world, so too, O Bhārata, does the Knower of the Field illumine the entire field. 13.33.
Śrīdhara: Because of its non-attachment, there is no taint; this has been shown by the illustration of space.
And because it is luminous, it is not joined with the attributes of that which is illuminated; this he states by the illustration of the sun in the verse beginning "just as [the sun] illuminates.
The meaning is clear.
Madhusūdana:

Not only is the Self not tainted because its nature is non-attachment, but because it is luminous, it is also not tainted by the attributes of the objects of illumination; thus he says "as" (*yathā*) with an illustration.
Just as the sun, though one alone, [illumines] this entire whole world—the aggregate of bodies and senses, and all material objects whatsoever—so too does the Self.
Thus, as long as it illuminates, it is neither stained by the qualities of that which is illuminated, nor is it divided by the diversity of that which is illuminated;
in the same way, O Bhārata, the Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña) is one alone and illuminates the entire field (kṣetra).
Therefore, the meaning is that it is neither stained by the qualities of the objects revealed, nor is it divided by the diversity of those objects;
just as the sun, the eye of the entire world, is not stained by external ocular defects.
In the same way, the one inner self of all beings is not tainted by the suffering of the world, being external to it.
Thus, according to the Vedic scripture [KaṭhU 2.2.11].
Viśvanātha says: "Because it is the illuminator, it is not joined with the qualities of the illuminated"; he states this with an illustration, beginning with "just as":
just as the sun, being the illuminator, is not joined with the qualities of the illuminated.
Likewise, the Field-knower, the Supreme Self,
is like the sun which, though it is the eye of the entire world, is not defiled by external defects of the eyes.
In the same way, the one inner self of all beings is not tainted by external grief or suffering.
Thus, according to the Vedic scripture [KaṭhU 2.2.11].
Baladeva: He says "as" (yathā) to show that the Self, though indeed untainted by the attributes of the body, sustains the body through its own attribute.

Just as the one sun illumines this entire world with its radiance, so too the one Knower of the Field—the individual soul (jīva)—illumines and makes conscious this entire field, the body, from the feet to the head, by means of consciousness; thus he speaks of it as being due to its quality.
Or, as in common worldly usage, according to [Pāṇini] Vs 2.3.26.

Those who, by means of the eye of knowledge, thus understand the distinction between the field and the Knower of the field, as well as the liberation from the material nature of beings, they go to the Supreme. 34.
Śrīdhara: He concludes the meaning of the chapter with the words "of the field and the knower of the field.

Those who, in the manner thus described, know the distinction—the difference—between the field and the knower of the field by means of the eye characterized by discriminative knowledge; and likewise [know] the "field," which is the nature (prakṛti) of beings, as well as liberation from it, namely the means to liberation such as meditation and so forth.
And those who know them go to the supreme state. //34//
I bow to that Lord, the son of Nanda, who is supreme bliss, by whose true essence primordial nature (prakṛti) and the person (puruṣa), though distinct, appear as if mixed.
Thus ends the thirteenth chapter, titled "The Yoga of the Discrimination between Matter and Spirit," in the *Subodhinī*, a commentary on the *Bhagavad-gītā* composed by the venerable Śrīdhara Svāmī.
Madhusūdana:
Now, he concludes the subject matter of the chapter with its fruit in the verse beginning with "kṣetra.
The difference—the mutual distinction—between the field (*kṣetra*) and the knower of the field (*kṣetrajña*), which were previously explained, is as described in the manner stated above.

Those who, with the eye of knowledge— consisting of self-knowledge produced by the instruction of the scriptures and the teacher— know this nature of dullness, consciousness, mutability, and immutability,

and know the liberation from the *prakṛti* (nature) of all beings— that is, the cessation through the supreme knowledge of the Self of that which is called *māyā* or ignorance— they go to the Supreme.
The meaning is that liberation (*kaivalya*) is the essential nature of the reality of the supreme Self; it does not, however, assume a body again.

Thus, it is established that for one who is steadfast in the means such as humility and possesses the discriminative knowledge of the field (*kṣetra*) and the knower of the field (*kṣetrajña*), there is the attainment of the supreme human goal through the cessation of all misfortunes. //34//

Thus ends the thirteenth chapter, titled "The Discrimination between the Field and the Knower of the Field," in the *Śrīmad-Bhagavad-Gītā-Gūḍhārtha-Dīpikā* (The Lamp Illuminating the Hidden Meaning of the Śrīmad-Bhagavad-Gītā), composed by the venerable Madhusūdana Sarasvatī, disciple of the venerable Paramahaṃsa Parivrājaka Ācārya Śrī Viśveśvara Sarasvatī.

Viśvanātha: He concludes the chapter with the words "those who know": those who know the distinction—the difference—between the knower of the field (kṣetrajña) and the field (kṣetra), namely the individual self (jīvātman) and the supreme self (paramātman); as well as the liberation of living beings from primordial nature (prakṛti), and the means to liberation, such as meditation and so forth.
They go to the supreme state. //34//
Between the two knowers of the field (kṣetrajña), the individual soul (jīvātman) partakes of the qualities of the field;
it is bound and liberated through knowledge—this is declared to be the meaning of the chapter.
Thus ends the thirteenth chapter, perfectly composed for the virtuous, in this delightful commentary that showers the essential meaning for those whose hearts are devoted. 13.
Baladeva: Concluding the meaning of the chapter, he states the fruit of that knowledge with the words "kṣetre" (in the field).

Those who, by means of the eye of knowledge—the vision consisting of wisdom regarding the distinction between the two Kṣetrajñas, namely the individual soul (jīva) and the Lord (īśa), which are conjoined with the field—know thus, according to the method of my teaching, their mutual difference and distinction, for such persons there is liberation from Prakṛti.

And those who know that means of attaining it—namely, humility and the other qualities—go to My abode, which is beyond material nature, the most excellent, known as the supreme ether (paravyoman). //34//

The individual soul and the Lord reside within the body; therein, the former is joined with the attributes of the body and is bound or liberated through awakening—this is the knowledge from the thirteenth chapter.
Thus ends the thirteenth chapter in the commentary on the Śrīmad-Bhagavad-Gītā Upaniṣad. //13//
